#31150. Is It True That The Boeing 747-8 & 787 Dreamliner Are Powered By The Same Engine?

Is It True That The Boeing 747-8 & 787 Dreamliner Are Powered By The Same Engine?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1345 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is true that both the 747-8, the final iteration of the Boeing double-decker, and the 787 Dreamliner, its latest and greatest clean sheet design, use the same engine.
  • The 747-8 exclusively uses the GEnx-2B while the 787 Dreamliner is the only jetliner to ever be equipped with the GEnx-1B.
  • Industry observers note that for airlines that operate both the 787 and 747-8, using the same engine family simplifies maintenance, parts inventory, and technician training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is true that both the 747-8, the final iteration of the Boeing double-decker, and the 787 Dreamliner, its latest and greatest clean sheet design, use the same engine. However, each of these aircraft uses a different variation of that same turbofan that is tailored to its unique needs and engineering qualities.

The 747-8 exclusively uses the GEnx-2B while the 787 Dreamliner is the only jetliner to ever be equipped with the GEnx-1B. Boeing chose the GEnx for the 747-8 primarily to modernize the aging jumbo jet with next-generation technology. Both aircraft feature distinctive serrated chevrons on the engine nacelles, which mix hot exhaust with cool air to significantly reduce noise.

Industry observers note that for airlines that operate both the 787 and 747-8, using the same engine family simplifies maintenance, parts inventory, and technician training. The GEnx-1B is a larger, more powerful, and more-electric engine designed for a modern twin-engine jet. The GEnx-2B is a smaller, simplified variant that incorporates traditional pneumatics to breathe life into the older 747 systems while providing modern fuel efficiency.

While the GEnx-1B (787) and GEnx-2B (747-8) share a common high-pressure core and 80% of their Line Replaceable Units, they are distinct engines optimized for different aircraft architectures. The most fundamental difference is how the engines interact with the aircraft's internal systems. The GEnx family is designed to stay on wing 20% longer than previous generations, with some fleet leaders exceeding 30,000 hours without a major overhaul.

Both engines offer approximately 15% better fuel efficiency than the older CF6 engines they replaced. Tom Levin, General Manager of the GEnx/CF6 engine product line at GE Aviation, commented on the engine's success when the 1,000th GEnx engine was developed in 2015.

Industry observers note that “The GEnx was the fastest selling engine in GE’s history, and now it is the fastest production ramp up of a GE widebody engine program. The GEnx engine has proven itself with outstanding performance and reliability.".

Industry observers note that the 787 uses a bleedless architecture where most systems are powered electrically. The 747-8 uses a traditional bleed-air system to power environmental controls and start the engines, requiring the GEnx-2B to include bleed-air ports. The GEnx-2B has fewer stages in the booster and low-pressure turbine, optimizing it for a four-engine configuration.

The Boeing 747-8, on the other hand, uses a traditional bleed air system. It must bleed high-pressure air from the compressor to power the 747’s pneumatic systems, including cabin pressurization and thermal anti-icing.

To fit the 747’s wing and ground clearance, the GEnx-2B has a smaller fan diameter, 105 inches, compared to the 787’s 111 inches. Because the 747-8 has four engines while the 787 has only two, the -2B is simplified internally to be lighter and more optimized for its lower per-engine thrust requirement. The -2B produces roughly 66,500 lbs of thrust, whereas the 787 variants can reach up to 76,100 lbs.

The GEnx-1B has more power because it is intended for a twin-engine aircraft (787) that must maintain performance in the event of an engine failure during takeoff. Because the GEnx-2B's power is distributed across four engines on the 747-8, its thrust rating is 66,500 lbf lower. Compared with older engines like the CF6, the GEnx-2B's technology improves fuel efficiency and cuts emissions by 15%.

Recent findings suggest that in contrast to the 1B, the GEnx-2B has de-staged components to maximize weight and performance for a four-engine setup. In contrast to the 1B's four stages, the 2B's low-pressure compressor has three stages. In the low-pressure turbine, the 1B has seven stages, whereas the 2B has six.

It has been revealed that compared with the 747-8, the 787 Dreamliner delivers bettereconomics and is much more efficient in the widebody market, as it is a lightweight twin-engine composite aircraft. These engineering variations determine their efficiency and commercial success. The 747 uses about 3,800 gallons of fuel per hour, while the 787 uses about 2,900 gallons. The 787-9 is extremely efficient, using approximately 2.31 liters per 100 km per passenger, which is significantly better than the 747-8's 2.82 liters per 100 km per passenger.

According to recent reports, boeing's Dreamliner also costs significantly less to operate, with a lower cost per available seat mile. Airlines typically prefer smaller twin-engine aircraft because they are less dangerous to fill and fly. The 787's design and performance have allowed it to thrive in the modern aviation market, while the 747-8 saw limited passenger orders before production ended in 2017 and the 747 assembly line fully shut down in 2023.

Industry observers note that the Dreamliner has essentially eliminated the conventional hub-and-spoke paradigm that made the 747 necessary. While the 747 required high passenger capacity to be successful, the 787's efficiency lets it cover the same distances with fewer seats, making it a better match for today's point-to-point market.

In a recent development, the 787's efficiency allows airlines to launch new, nonstop point-to-point routes that would not have been economically viable with older, bigger, four-engine planes. Despite being more efficient than previous 747s, the 747-8 is still best suited to high-volume hub-to-hub services. Airlines such as United have made large 787 orders to replace a mix of 747s, 767s, and early 777s with a single, simpler aircraft family, resulting in significant cost savings for pilot training and component inventory.

Sources indicate that the 787 incorporates a large amount of carbon composite material, making it lighter, more resistant to fatigue and corrosion, and allowing for higher cabin humidity and lower cabin altitude, which enhances passenger comfort and reduces structural stress. The 747-8 is a development of a traditional aluminum design, with a heavier base structure.

Lufthansa has incorporated the 787-9 to handle flights that need the same range but have about 70–90 fewer people, even though it is still a 747-8 operator. Because of this, even at off-peak times, the airline can maintain high load factors (percentage of seats filled). British Airways switched to the 787-10 for important transatlantic flights to New York and Chicago after retiring its entire 747 fleet. The 787-10 is 25% more fuel-efficient than the 747 while offering comparable cargo capacity and contemporary comforts.

Compared to the 747, the 787 Dreamliner offers a better long-haul passenger experience because its composite airframe creates a cabin environment that more closely resembles ground conditions. When compared to older aircraft like the 747, which have a cabin altitude of 8,000 feet, the 787's cabin altitude of 6,000 feet makes a significant difference for passengers. That lower cabin altitude does many things to reduce the effects of fatigue on passengers inflight.

The composite construction of the 787 is not only 50% by weight but 80% by volume. Thanks to that light yet incredibly durable construction, it can do things no previous aircraft could. That includes having larger windows, higher humidity (15% or double that of legacy jets), and a more spacious interior with more natural lighting and better overhead storage.

According to recent reports, while the 747 is much loved for its incredibly smooth landing characteristics and gentle handling and flight, the 787 uses a latest technology known as 'smooth ride' to counteract turbulence in flight. This is the same technology that the 777X will use when it finally debuts in 2027. Although the 747 was known as the Queen of the Skies, the Dreamliner has become the best-selling widebody in history. It has been the flagship product of the legendary plane maker, as its 737 MAX has flailed in the wake of a disastrous debut.

This is not only a major improvement for the long-haul market, but also for operators that use these aircraft for high-density hub-to-hub transport, and makes a major improvement for the densest routes in the world. A 787 Dreamliner is not only a game-changer for the operators that fly it, but it also marks a paradigm shift in the experience for flyers. While the era of the 747 ushered in a golden age of jet-powered commercial aviation, the 787 and future successors such as the 777X herald the next era in air travel.

Industry News: Tempers flare as future of Social Security debated

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (685 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ron Johnson, R-Wis., mentioned he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).
  • If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.
  • Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., mentioned he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.

Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

“I think it’s outrageous,” noted Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking notable.”.

Johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

It has been revealed that "This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he noted on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”.

But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”.

In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson said Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”.

Industry observers note that johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he mentioned.

Industry observers note that there is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson said Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

It has been revealed that A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a initiative in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

According to recent reports, senators on both sides of the aisle remarked they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

“I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability issue, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” remarked Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’d like to think that I’m pretty understanding of airlines, and how they can fall short.
  • At the same time, sometimes there are situations where airlines act in a way that feels to me a little like theft.
  • Several weeks ago, I booked a ticket on Tunisair in business class from Tunis (TUN) to Marseille (MRS).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’d like to think that I’m pretty understanding of airlines, and how they can fall short. The airline industry is incredibly complex and low margin, and sometimes consumers have unrealistically high expectations, while not acknowledging the real cost and challenges of running an airline. Buying a ticket on a flight is more like buying a ticket on Amtrak than buying a night at a Four Seasons, and you should adjust expectations accordingly.

At the same time, sometimes there are situations where airlines act in a way that feels to me a little like theft. Readers often share these stories with me, and I write about them when I can. Now I’d like to share my own story….

Several weeks ago, I booked a ticket on Tunisair in business class from Tunis (TUN) to Marseille (MRS). A few days before the flight I received an email from Tunisair informing me that I had been downgraded. As it turns out, it was because my flight was swapped to a wet leased plane, in an all-economy layout.

According to recent reports, the email informed me of this change without actually acknowledging it was a downgrade. Instead, the email was in French, and it translated to “we are writing to inform you that your flight reservation has undergone changes.” And the only reference to the downgrade was that the fare class only demonstrated as being “Y,” which obviously isn’t business class.

There was zero other proactive communication from the airline about the incident, and I flew the flight in economy. The airline of course acted as if nothing happened, and there was no mention of how to request downgrade compensation, or anything like that.

It has been revealed that after the flight, I submitted a request with customer service, asking for a refund for the fare difference. Making that request was a challenge in and of itself, because the customer service form is in French, and is not at all intuitive.

Sources indicate that but anyway, it has been weeks, and I haven’t heard back. I’m a bit conflicted here. I try not to abuse credit card disputes, but you typically only have 60 days to file a dispute. So am I at the point where I should just file a dispute, or how would one handle that?

According to recent reports, as I said above, I try to be pretty understanding of airlines, and recognize how many different scenarios there are. Just in terms of doing business ethically, I do feel like there should be a proactive refund offer if the airline is informing you in advance that you won’t be getting the product that you paid for. I mean, if you can inform me that I’ve been downgraded, you can also process some sort of a refund.

We’ve become desensitized to this kind of service level with airlines, but I’m trying to come up with a comparison. I guess it would be like buying premium tickets to a sporting event, being informed in advance that you’ll be given worse seats, and then customer service just not responding to you for weeks on end.

If you managed to take my money, surely you can also manage to give it back if you can’t give me the thing I paid for, no?

Tunisair informed me days before a flight that I had been downgraded (as it turns out, due to an aircraft swap), though there was no offer a refund for a fare difference, or anything. Weeks ago I sent an email to customer service asking for a refund for the fare difference, but I haven’t heard back.

It just strikes me as really unethical to take someone’s money for an experience you’re not going to offer, and then not have a way to get a refund in a reasonable timeframe. I know airlines hate when people file credit card disputes, but when you’re approaching the 60-day mark with no response, what is one supposed to do?

Am I the only one who thinks it’s ridiculous to proactively downgrade a customer, but then make getting a refund such a runaround?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, hyatt will bring its luxury Park Hyatt brand to Brisbane, Australia.
    • Hyatt has confirmed intends for the Park Hyatt Brisbane, marking the brand’s debut in Queensland.
    • The hotel will occupy the top floors of one of the two towers of the 309 North Quay, a mixed-use development also containing luxury homes and retail outlets.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, hyatt will bring its luxury Park Hyatt brand to Brisbane, Australia. More Park Hyatt locations are always a good thing, but… well, let’s cover the details first.

    Hyatt has confirmed intends for the Park Hyatt Brisbane, marking the brand’s debut in Queensland. The hotel is expected to open in 2031, and will be located on the shores of the Brisbane River, at the western edge of the city’s central business district.

    The hotel will occupy the top floors of one of the two towers of the 309 North Quay, a mixed-use development also containing luxury homes and retail outlets. For what it’s worth, the two buildings will have 51 floors and 56 floors. The hotel will have 201 guest rooms and suites, offering views of the river and skyline, along with 50 serviced apartments, for extended residence.

    Sources indicate that there are no additional details about the property yet. I do appreciate that the hotel will at least be at the top of a building, as that should make for some very nice views (I hate when hotels are part of tall buildings, but then take up the bottom floors, as that’s becoming increasingly common).

    While a 2031 opening is expected, I would definitely not count on that timeline sticking. Ground hasn’t even broken on this development, and these kinds of mixed-use developments tend to struggle with sticking to their planned timeline.

    Here’s how Tamara Lohan, Hyatt’s Global Brand Leader for Luxury, describes this:.

    “The Park Hyatt calling cards have always been iconic design and extraordinary addresses. Brisbane has the confidence and growing global pull to make it a natural home for the brand. When it opens, Park Hyatt Brisbane will become the fifth Park Hyatt hotel in the Pacific, joining hotels in Sydney, Melbourne, Canberra and Auckland, and a deliberate next step in growing the brand in the right places.”.

    There are no renderings of the property yet, beyond the below one of the overall 309 North Quay development.

    In a recent development, this will be the fourth Park Hyatt property in Australia, and the fifth in the South Pacific, complementing the properties in Auckland, Canberra, Melbourne, and Sydney. I don’t have the slightest clue what’s going on with the Canberra property, as my understanding is that it’s not up to Park Hyatt standards, so it’s marketed as “Hyatt Hotel Canberra – A Park Hyatt Hotel.” So it is a Park Hyatt, or is it not a Park Hyatt?

    Recent findings suggest that world of Hyatt is my favorite major hotel loyalty program (though the lead is narrowing as of late), and Park Hyatt is probably my favorite Hyatt brand. 15 years ago, the brand got me really excited, because it had some really spectacular properties. But it just feels like the brand is sort of losing steam, especially when you compare the difference in trajectory between Park Hyatt and Waldorf Astoria. My frustration with Park Hyatt comes down to two things.

    First, the brand just seemingly can’t pick up many “flagship” properties, or at least can’t maintain them. Look at the world’s biggest business markets and most iconic cities — we’re talking Hong Kong, London, New York, Paris, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, etc. There are no Park Hyatts in places like Hong Kong or Singapore, and the ones that have historically been pretty iconic just fall short of actually being the top properties in their cities:.

    The area where Park Hyatt has been doing well in recent times is in secondary cities, at least in comparison to the above. And this isn’t meant to be shade — I’d much rather hang out in Auckland or Kuala Lumpur than in London or New York (take your pitchforks elsewhere!), but there’s no denying that any true luxury hotel brand wants to have world class properties in those primary cities.

    I just feel like as of late, Waldorf Astoria’s trajectory has been way more impressive than Park Hyatt’s, and I’m not sure what exactly is driving that. I feel like owners just aren’t as into developing Park Hyatts as they used to be. Is there a single Park Hyatt in the pipeline where I think “oh, this is going to be a best-in-class property in a major market?” I can’t think of any….

    The Park Hyatt brand is coming to Brisbane, Australia, with a hotel expected to open in 2031. The 201-key property will be located on the top floors of a mixed-use development, which will also contain apartments and retail.

    According to recent reports, it’s cool to see more Park Hyatts in the pipeline, and I don’t want to knock the brand for expanding to more markets. I’m just disappointed that the Park Hyatt brand can’t pick up any steam in the biggest cities, in terms of delivering an actually competitive experience.

    #31144. The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1626 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1626 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that article II, Section 1 of the Constitution sets out the process by which Americans select their president.
    • Democrats have been railing against the Electoral College since losing the 2000 and 2016 elections while winning a plurality of the popular vote.
    • Recent findings suggest that A proposed workaround has sailed through the legislatures of 18 blue states and the District of Columbia: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that article II, Section 1 of the Constitution sets out the process by which Americans select their president. Alexander Hamilton marveled at the time, in Federalist No. 68, that it was “almost the only part of the system, of any consequence, which has escaped without severe censure, or which has received the slightest mark of approbation from its opponents.” The core of that process is that the members of the Electoral College are selected in each state. With only the Twelfth Amendment’s modification in 1804 to adjust how the vice president is selected, this same system has been in continuous use for 238 years. It is how George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Ronald Reagan, and Barack Obama were elected. Now, a nefarious plot aims to overthrow the American system.

    Democrats have been railing against the Electoral College since losing the 2000 and 2016 elections while winning a plurality of the popular vote. These partisan sour grapes have often been dismissed as empty talk because the Electoral College is established by the Constitution, so only an amendment could abolish it. An amendment requires a two-thirds vote of Congress and the consent of 38 states, both of which are out of reach on a party-line vote.

    Recent findings suggest that A proposed workaround has sailed through the legislatures of 18 blue states and the District of Columbia: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. The theory is that these states would award their electors not to the winner of the popular vote in their own state, but to the winner of the national popular vote. It may be that a state can decide on its own to do this. States have not always picked electors by statewide popular vote. Many states at the Founding had their state legislatures choose electors. South Carolina did so all the way to the Civil War. Colorado in 1876 was the last state to do so, but only because it had just been admitted to statehood and claimed not to have time to organize a statewide vote. Other states have awarded electors to the winners of each House district, as Maine and Nebraska do today; this system was upheld by the Supreme Court in 1892.

    According to recent reports, but the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact is not just a unilateral decision by individual states about how to award their electors. If it had been, it would already have been effective in 2024, and Donald Trump would have won the Electoral College 530–8 with 49.7 percent of the popular vote. Instead, it is styled as an agreement that goes into effect only if states composing a majority of the Electoral College approve it. At present, the signatories control 222 electoral votes. With Democrats gaining trifectas in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, and Arizona, they conceivably could pass the compact in states controlling 283 electoral votes. They also now control the New Hampshire state legislature, although with a veto-proof majority only in one of its two chambers, they would have to get through Republican Governor Kelly Ayotte.

    Passage is not certain. Michigan Democrats have previously rejected the compact in 2023 and 2024, and in Nevada (a smaller state that would be swamped under the compact), the Democratic governor vetoed it in 2019. Some of the small-state signatories, such as Delaware, Vermont, Rhode Island, or Latest Mexico, might yet have second thoughts now that they are playing with live ammunition.

    It has been revealed that moreover, under Article I, Section 10, interstate compacts require the consent of Congress. Even if Democrats passed it in the next two years with the aim of changing the rules for the 2028 election, Trump would surely veto it. After the 2030 Census, a number of the signatory states are expected to lose House seats, which will further narrow the margin for keeping it in effect. Then, there’s the question of whether the Supreme Court would allow individual states to gang up and effectively nullify the entire constitutional design of our presidential election system.

    Industry observers note that legal obstacles aside, this is a bad idea. To start with, the very durability of our system over such a long period is an argument in its favor. No other nation has used the same system for choosing its head of state and government for so long. Leaving aside the dubious precedents of 1824 (when popular vote records were not kept in the most populous state) and 1876 (when fraud was rampant in both parties and Southern Democrats engaged in mass violence against Republican voters), the Electoral College has only delivered a different outcome from the national popular vote three times in our history. In each case, the national vote was fairly close and neither candidate got a popular majority, so the Electoral College provided the legitimacy of a majority result that the popular vote could not. This may have frustrated Californians, but it was not just the tyranny of a few small places with no people in them. In 2016, Trump won the popular vote in seven of the ten largest states. It is nearly impossible to win a national popular majority without carrying the Electoral College.

    Sources indicate that we have an Electoral College because we are a nation of diverse and distinct states. The American people are long accustomed to this system. The people ratified the Constitution and its amendments state-by-state. The Senate is elected by the people in states, the House by people in districts. Both political parties choose their presidential nominees by primary elections in each state. Americans have never before held a nationwide popular vote for any purpose. Our election systems, run by state and local officials with a variety of rules for the timing of casting and counting ballots and for confirming the qualifications of voters, are not designed for such a vote.

    Recent findings suggest that our campaigns today still prioritize appeals to the most closely divided states. This encourages presidential candidates to pitch at least some of their message to voters in the center, and also to travel the country in order to garner coverage in statewide media and the support of state and local power brokers. A national popular vote campaign would drive us even further down the road of nationalizing the campaign media environment and encouraging candidates to rally voters in their party’s strongholds. It would also exacerbate the divide between urban and rural or small-town America, given how the largest cities could effectively ally themselves against their own in-state neighbors.

    According to recent reports, few of the world’s democracies conduct a nationwide vote for the chief executive. In France, which is one of those, the first man to win such a vote seized power in a coup before his first term ended. National popular plebiscites are far more common in dictatorial systems, where the president has more control over who counts the votes. One of the reasons why the January 6 mob was never a serious threat to overturn the 2020 election was that the state-by-state winners had already been publicly certified in 50 separate state capitals. This was a deliberate feature of the system: As Hamilton wrote, “as the electors, chosen in each State, are to assemble and vote in the State in which they are chosen, this detached and divided situation will expose them much less to heats and ferments . . . than if they were all to be convened at one time, in one place.”.

    In a recent development, we would inevitably need to overhaul our entire election system to accommodate a nationwide vote. It is not a coincidence that such a nationalization of elections is favored by many of the same people who want to do away with the Electoral College. As things stand today, the whole country would have to wait on California, which not only takes weeks to count votes, but does so in order to count late-arriving ballots and to “cure” defective ballots — a process bound to erode confidence in a close election. That matters little when nobody doubts the outcome in California. But by making elections turn on the margins of victory in the deepest-blue or deepest-red jurisdictions, whose election officials are uniformly of the same party, the incentives for all manner of electoral malfeasance would be supercharged.

    Recent findings suggest that the 1888 election provides a vivid, if extreme, example of how the Electoral College limits the scope of mischief done by the corruption of voting systems in particular states. The eleven states of the former Confederacy were then well into the post-Reconstruction suppression of the black vote in their states. As a result, the Democratic nominee, Grover Cleveland, won those states by almost 25 points, with over 60 percent of the vote. This propelled Cleveland to a narrow plurality in the national popular vote even though his Republican opponent, Benjamin Harrison, won a popular majority in the rest of the country. Yet the Electoral College gave Harrison the victory because his support was not as concentrated in an unrepresentative handful of states in which the vote was compromised.

    In a recent development, if a nationwide vote would be a headache, a nationwide recount would be a nightmare. Nobody who lived through the 2000 and 2020 post-election controversies should have any illusions that such a thing could be conducted in a civil and orderly fashion in today’s America. Rather than wait to learn that lesson the hard way, we should step back from the brink of overthrowing the system that has chosen our nation’s leader from the beginning.

    The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

    #31143. Fun & Creative Airline Callsigns, From Shamrock To Starwalker

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1330 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Fun & Creative Airline Callsigns, From Shamrock To Starwalker

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1330 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Here’s a fun topic for aviation geeks (so if you’re not one, feel free to skip this post)….
    • When pilots and air traffic controllers communicate, they have a callsign that they use to be identified.
    • In general aviation, that callsign is just the aircraft’s registration code, so it’s always the same for a particular aircraft.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Here’s a fun topic for aviation geeks (so if you’re not one, feel free to skip this post)….

    When pilots and air traffic controllers communicate, they have a callsign that they use to be identified.

    In general aviation, that callsign is just the aircraft’s registration code, so it’s always the same for a particular aircraft. For example, if the plane has the registration code N111PG, it would be spoken as “November One One One Papa Golf.”.

    Sources indicate that meanwhile for commercial aircraft, the callsign consists of a tech giant identifier plus the flight number. In some cases that company identifier is simply the company’s name, while in other cases, a different callsign is used. For example, for American, Delta, and United, the company identifier is simply the airline name, so American flight 100 would be spoken as “American 100.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in some situations, airlines choose callsigns that are different from the company name, and this can be for a variety of reasons. Callsigns need to be approved by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), with some vital considerations:.

    In a recent development, while most airlines simply use their name as their callsign, there are also some airlines that don’t, and there are some names that I find to be particularly fun. In this post, I’d like to share my favorite airline callsigns, with a little backstory on how they were chosen (as I understand it). In no particular order….

    Industry observers note that aer Lingus’ callsign is “Shamrock,” and that’s because the shamrock is the national symbol of Ireland. It’s a key part of the airline’s corporate identity, down to the shamrock being featured on the tails of Aer Lingus planes.

    Sources indicate that british Airways’ callsign is “Speedbird,” and I’d argue it’s perhaps the most iconic callsign out there. The origin of this dates back to British Airways’ predecessor, Imperial Airways, which used the stylized bird logo. British Airways has been using the callsign since it was founded in 1974 (as a combination of predecessors).

    While this is of course a creative callsign, it has a practical use as well. “British Airways” would’ve been too long of a callsign, and “British” would’ve likely been too generic. For example, British Midland (which ended up being merged into British Airways) used “Midland” as its callsign, to avoid confusion.

    In a recent development, republic Airways’ callsign is “Brickyard,” and it’s probably the coolest callsign you’ll find at an airline in the United States. The callsign is a tribute to the company’s headquarters in Indianapolis, also home to the Indianapolis Motor Speedway. The course was initially paved with three million bricks, and nicknamed “The Brickyard.”.

    For those not familiar, Republic operates flights on behalf of the regional subsidiaries of the major US carriers, so this is among the most common callsigns you’ll hear on air traffic control frequencies in the US.

    Recent findings suggest that PSA Airlines’ callsign is “Blue Streak,” and after Republic, it’s probably the coolest callsign you’ll find at an airline in the United States. The story behind this callsign is definitely a blast from the past. In the 1980s, PSA’s predecessor was Jetstream International Airlines, and it operated commuter flights as a Piedmont Commuter feeder carrier.

    The carrier’s planes had a white fuselage with a prominent blue stripe along it, intended to match Piedmont Airlines’ livery, and that’s where it all started.

    For those not familiar, PSA operates flights on behalf of the regional subsidiaries of the major US carriers, so this is also a very common callsign that you’ll hear. Given the lack of blue stripes nowadays, the callsign does tend to cause some confusion!

    China Airlines’ callsign is “Dynasty.” It’s my understanding that the Taiwan-based carrier had to choose a non-obvious callsign both to avoid confusion (given the number of airlines with “China” in their name), and also with the intent of differentiating it from mainland China.

    In a recent development, so, where did the dynasty term come from? China Airlines uses this branding pretty widely, with its frequent flyer program even being named Dynasty Flyer, and it’s intended to reflect the history of Taiwan.

    Starlux Airlines’ callsign is “Starwalker.” The reason is because the “Starlux” callsign was already taken by Comlux Aruba, a tiny charter airline, before the Taiwanese airline was founded. Now, don’t ask me why Comlux Aruba has “Starlux” as its callsign, though!

    The reason Starlux ended up with “Starwalker” is presumably because the manufacturer’s founder is a huge Star Wars fan, which is why many things about the airline have space branding. He’s also of course a huge aviation geek, and operates flights as a captain!

    According to recent reports, south African Airways’ callsign is “Springbok.” The reason is because “South African” would be too long of a callsign, so they selected the springbok, which is the national animal of South Africa. The carrier has also used this in its branding over the years. For example, back in the 1950s, the airline used “Springbok Service” to describe its long haul, flagship flights.

    According to recent reports, atlas Air’s callsign is “Giant.” Huh, say what? For those not familiar, Atlas Air is a cargo and charter airline, and while it doesn’t operate regularly scheduled commercial flights, it is a big operation.

    Industry observers note that the callsign is presumably a reflection of the company’s name coming from Greek mythology, where “Atlas” was a titan of great strength, so that may also explain the “giant” callsign. Now, it’s worth mentioning that Atlas also flies some pretty “giant” planes, as the world’s largest Boeing 747 operator, but I don’t think that’s the primary motivation.

    Kalitta Air’s callsign is “Connie.” For those not familiar, Kalitta Air is a cargo airline with a few dozen planes (most of which are Boeing 747s!). The callsign is named after the company’s founder, Conrad “Connie” Kalitta, who started the airline back in 1967, as Connie Kalitta Services.

    European Air Transport’s callsign is “Postman.” For context, this is one of DHL’s European subsidiaries operating cargo flights, so it’s a pretty fitting callsign, eh?

    Airlines have callsigns that they use to communicate with air traffic control. While most airlines simply use their name as their callsign, that’s not always the case. In some situations a different name has to be chosen for practical reasons, while in some cases airlines want to get creative. I love when airlines have some fun with this, so I figured it was worth a post.

    What’s your favorite airline callsign?

    #31142. Why Are All Pratt & Whitney's GTF Engines Green On The Inside?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1628 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Are All Pratt & Whitney's GTF Engines Green On The Inside?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1628 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that passengers boarding an Airbus A320neo or an A220 who glance at the engine intake from the jet bridge often notice something unusual.
    • It has been revealed that the more convincing answers sit in materials science and maintenance practice.
    • The broad green band lining the inner surface of the fan case is the engine’s acoustic liner, a panel built from a perforated skin bonded over a honeycomb core.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that passengers boarding an Airbus A320neo or an A220 who glance at the engine intake from the jet bridge often notice something unusual. Inside the nacelle, ahead of the fan blades, a ring of teal green lines the casing of the Pratt & Whitney Geared Turbofan, whether the aircraft carries the PW1100G of the A320neo family or the PW1500G of the A220. The color is consistent enough across the fleet that spotters and online aviation communities have debated its purpose for years, with explanations ranging from branding to corrosion protection.

    It has been revealed that the more convincing answers sit in materials science and maintenance practice. Two separate components contribute to the green appearance, each with its own function and its own reason for the shade it carries, and a third factor, the practical needs of the people who inspect the engines, explains why the color has persisted. Examining those components in turn clarifies how a modern geared turbofan manages noise, tip clearance, and inspection, and why a seemingly cosmetic detail reflects engineering decisions made well before the engine reaches an airline.

    The broad green band lining the inner surface of the fan case is the engine’s acoustic liner, a panel built from a perforated skin bonded over a honeycomb core. The perforations admit sound waves into the cells of the honeycomb, where each cell behaves like a small resonant chamber that absorbs acoustic energy and converts a portion of it into heat. By sizing the cells and the perforated face sheet for particular frequencies, designers tune the panel to dampen the tones that dominate fan noise.

    The geared architecture makes this component especially relevant. Because a reduction gearbox lets the fan turn more slowly than the turbine driving it, the engine produces a different acoustic signature from a direct-drive fan of similar size, with more of the energy at lower frequencies. Low-frequency sound is harder to absorb than high-frequency sound, since longer wavelengths need deeper cavities to dissipate effectively, which is why the liner occupies a generous stretch of the inlet. Pratt & Whitney has promoted the engine’s reduced noise footprint as a headline benefit, and the liner is one of several features that contribute to it alongside the slower fan itself.

    Construction follows a sandwich principle common to aerospace structures. A solid backing sheet closes one side of the honeycomb, and the perforated face sheet closes the other. The arrangement delivers acoustic performance with very little weight, a priority in any component carried on an engine hanging from the wing, where added mass raises fuel burn. The panels are also designed to withstand airflow, vibration, temperature swings, and minor debris impacts throughout a long service life.

    The teal shade is generally attributed to the composite itself rather than to a decorative coating. According to descriptions of the construction, the resin and epoxy matrix that bind the liner’s layers carry a natural pigmentation that demonstrates through on the finished surface. Engineers have a practical reason to avoid covering it. A thick film of paint would partially fill the microscopic perforations in the face sheet, reducing the open area through which sound enters the cavities and degrading the attenuation the panel was designed to achieve.

    However, this explanation should be treated with some caution, because there has not been a published manufacturer statement regarding the color. As a result, the exact origin of the hue remains an informed inference rather than a documented fact. The uniform result across A320neo and A220 installations nonetheless suggests a controlled material choice instead of an incidental one.

    Industry observers note that directly aft of the acoustic ring sits a slightly lighter blue-green band, the abradable rub strip, which technical literature also calls a fan outer air seal. Its job is to control the gap between the fan blade tips and the surrounding case. Any air that leaks across that gap represents lost work, so engine makers want the clearance as small as practical without allowing the blades to strike a hard surface.

    Sources indicate that the abradable material solves that problem by being softer than the blade tips. During break-in, the tips cut a shallow groove into the strip, producing a seal matched to the actual shape of that particular fan, including any slight growth caused by heat and centrifugal loading. The strip wears while the blades and the case remain intact. A paper from the 2003 NASA Seal/Secondary Air System Workshop, which covers Pratt & Whitney abradable seals, documents the broader engineering approach behind such materials.

    Sources indicate that the color of this strip carries its own explanation. The compound is supplied as a two-part epoxy and hardener, and the components are mixed to a defined turquoise shade so that a uniform color confirms the two parts were blended properly before application. Streaks or patches of a different tone would signal incomplete mixing, and with it a risk that the cured strip will not abrade predictably. The compound’s behavior over time matters as much as its initial performance. As the engine accumulates cycles, the strip gradually erodes from airflow, particles, and repeated light contact, and clearance grows accordingly. Operators therefore monitor the condition of the strip during scheduled inspections and restore it when wear exceeds published limits, a process that depends on repeating the same mixing and curing steps, and the same color check, each time the material is applied.

    Beyond material chemistry, the saturated green interior gives maintenance crews a practical advantage during walk-around checks. The fan case sits in a shadowed cavity, and the blades, the hub, and any dark residue around the casing can blend together in poor light. A bright, uniform background makes departures from normal appearance easier to see.

    Ramp inspectors look for several conditions in this region. Foreign object debris, such as fragments of tire, packing material, or bird remains, stands out against the green surface. Erosion of the liner or the rub strip shows as lighter patches or exposed honeycomb, and abnormal wear on the blade tips appears as unusual rub patterns where the strip has been cut. Because these checks often occur between flights under airport lighting and on tight schedules, a background that makes anomalies obvious reduces the chance of a missed finding.

    Industry observers note that the choice of green also reflects how the human eye distinguishes color. Green sits near the middle of the visible spectrum, where daylight vision is most sensitive, and it contrasts strongly with the reds, browns, and oranges typical of oil, hydraulic fluid, and corrosion products, so a stain or deposit on the liner is easier to notice than it would be on a gray or white surface.

    Industry observers note that the GTF is far from the first aircraft component to appear in this color. Aerospace suppliers have long finished parts in green, and BMT Aerospace notes that the shade is often traced to protective primers applied to metal surfaces to resist corrosion. Zinc chromate primer, widely used for decades on airframes and components, has a distinctive yellow-green tone, which is why green surfaces are a familiar sight inside wheel wells, wing bays, and equipment racks.

    Public discussion has also linked the GTF’s green interior to Pratt & Whitney’s environmental positioning, since the engine is marketed on lower fuel burn, reduced emissions, and quieter operation. This reading is plausible as a secondary benefit but lacks documentary support, and the engineering explanations above are sufficient on their own. A color that doubles as a reminder of the engine’s efficiency claims costs the manufacturer nothing, which may be why no one has felt a need to change it.

    In a recent development, the green interior of the GTF is a small example of a larger trend in which material properties are doing more of the work that markings once did. As engines move toward larger, slower fans housed in shorter nacelles, liners will have to absorb more sound from less surface area, which pushes designers toward more sophisticated core geometries and multilayer constructions. Pratt & Whitney’s improved GTF Advantage variant retains the same gearbox architecture, so the existing liner conventions should carry forward into the newer engines.

    It has been revealed that inspection practice is also changing. Airlines and maintenance providers are adopting borescope automation, drone-assisted visual checks, and machine-vision software that compares images against a reference baseline. A controlled, repeatable color simplifies that comparison, because software can flag deviations in hue or texture more reliably when the underlying surface is uniform. Should manufacturers publish color tolerances for liners and rub strips, the green interior could evolve from an informal convention into a formal measurement reference, with deviations scored automatically before a technician reaches the engine.

    Material choices will also respond to environmental scrutiny. Chromate-based primers are under regulatory pressure in several jurisdictions because of worker exposure and disposal concerns, and the industry is moving toward alternatives. Any substitute for current coatings will need to preserve acoustic openness, bonding strength, and the visual contrast that crews rely on, which may lead suppliers to add deliberate pigments where natural color once sufficed.

    Recent findings suggest that for the existing fleet, the near-term picture is straightforward. With a large and growing fleet in service, the teal ring is likely to remain a recognizable feature for decades, and its meaning will rest on data as much as on appearance. Operators who record inspection images consistently over an engine’s life will build a visual history of wear that could support condition-based maintenance, replacing fixed intervals with decisions informed by measured trends in clearance and liner condition. In that sense, the color’s greatest value may lie ahead of it, as a standardized backdrop for the analytics that will govern how these engines are maintained.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • LATAM has just unveiled the full interiors for its upcoming Airbus A321XLRs, which will make it the first carrier in South America to offer fully flat suites with direct aisle access on a narrow body aircraft.
    • LATAM has 13 Airbus A321XLRs are on order, which are expected to enter service as of March 2027.
    • It has been revealed that the airline intends to use these planes to open up newly introduced long haul markets, though it’s not yet clear out of which LATAM hubs the planes will fly.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    LATAM has just unveiled the full interiors for its upcoming Airbus A321XLRs, which will make it the first carrier in South America to offer fully flat suites with direct aisle access on a narrow body aircraft. These planes are expected to enter service in the coming months, so we won’t have to wait much longer to fly them!

    LATAM has 13 Airbus A321XLRs are on order, which are expected to enter service as of March 2027. The A321XLR is the newly introduced long range, narrow body aircraft from Airbus, which stretches the capabilities of the A321 family.

    It has been revealed that the airline intends to use these planes to open up newly introduced long haul markets, though it’s not yet clear out of which LATAM hubs the planes will fly. I suspect these planes will primarily be used for service to North America, or possibly for service from secondary cities in Brazil to Europe. Officially, for now the airline just claims these planes will be used to “strengthen connectivity between South America and more distant destinations.”.

    Earlier this year, LATAM’s CEO did drop some hints that the plane could fly from Lima (LIM) and Brasilia (BSB) to the United States, and from Fortaleza (FOR) to Europe, though no final decisions have been announced.

    According to recent reports, we can expect LATAM to offer an all-new passenger experience (by the carrier’s standards) onboard the Airbus A321XLRs. The airline intends to configure the planes with a total of 174 seats, including:.

    Throughout the plane, passengers can expect the Panasonic Astrova entertainment system, with over 2,300 hours of content, including 330 movies and 1,200 TV shows. Bluetooth audio will also be available at all seats, so that passengers can connect to their own headphones. The A321XLR will also be equipped with SES Wi-Fi, with LATAM Pass members getting complimentary browsing or messaging, depending on their membership tier and ticket type.

    LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product. So there will be 12 herringbone seats in a 1-1 configuration, with seats spread across six rows. This means all seats will have direct aisle access and doors. Business class seats will feature 19″ 4K OLED screens, AC power outlets, USB-C charging, and wireless charging.

    Recent findings suggest that it also looks like the front row seats will be pretty special, as they’ll feature quite a bit of extra space, including a closet and wardrobe. It remains to be seen how the airline will monetize that extra space, if at all (maybe they’ll just be reserved for certain types of passengers?).

    It has been revealed that LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Recaro R3 product. So there will be 162 seats in a 3-3 configuration, with six rows having extra legroom, and 21 rows having standard legroom. Economy class seats will feature 13″ 4K OLED screens, as well as USB-C outlets.

    In a recent development, the A321XLR is impressive for its range, and it’s understandable that the economics of such a small plane for long haul flying can be challenging. As a result, we’re really seeing airlines try to maximize capacity as much as possible, and this is also leading to so many airlines having very similar premium products on planes.

    LATAM will have herringbone seats on the A321XLR, just like… well, all current operators that use this primarily as a long haul aircraft, with the exception of Aer Lingus.

    For those keeping track at home, the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product is what you’ll find in JetBlue’s Mint business class on select A321neo/LR aircraft, and it’s also what you’ll find in Iberia’s A321XLR business class.

    Recent findings suggest that while American’s A321XLR business class looks similar, it’s based on the Collins Aerospace Aurora seating platform, and that’s also what Air Canada has selected. Meanwhile United’s A321XLR business class also looks similar, but is based on the Elevate Altitude platform.

    According to recent reports, admittedly these planes all have better business class products than we found on long haul Boeing 757s years ago (the most direct replacement), and the tech is also greatly updated. That being noted, as a passenger experience geek, this sure is a boring plane… “you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, everyone gets a herringbone seat!”.

    While not quite A321XLRs, credit to ITA Airways’ A321neo business class and Etihad’s A321LR business class for having reverse herringbone seats.

    To LATAM’s credit, I will say that the cabin finishes look gorgeous, so I hope they look as nice in real life as they do in renderings.

    Sources indicate that in early 2027, LATAM expects to start taking delivery of the Airbus A321XLR, which the airline looks to use to grow into new markets. The airline has now revealed what we can expect onboard these planes, and it includes herringbone seats with direct aisle access and doors in business class.

    It has been revealed that ultimately the cabin looks sleek, and it’s cool to see this in South America, where no other airline is at the moment offering such an experience. But still, it’s hard to get too excited when so many airlines are introducing a similar product.

    LATAM in general deserves credit for the extent to which it’s elevating the passenger experience in Latin America, as we’ve seen the airline introduce two new wide body business class products over the past several years.

    What do you make of LATAM’s upcoming A321XLR business class?

    Tech Report: Citi Shop offers an easier way to save when shopping online

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that citi Shop takes some of the work out of saving money online.
    • It has broad reach, too, with more than 5,000 participating online merchants.
    • Its ease of use makes it a great resource, but other portals or special discounts may save you more.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that citi Shop takes some of the work out of saving money online. Once you've installed its browser extension, it acts as a shopping portal and coupon hunter all-in-one, rewarding you with statement credits.

    It has broad reach, too, with more than 5,000 participating online merchants. That's easier than a traditional online shopping portal, which requires you to remember to start at the portal and click through before filling your cart.

    Its ease of use makes it a great resource, but other portals or special discounts may save you more.

    Here's how Citi Shop works and what to consider to determine if it's the best savings path for you.

    In a recent development, citi Shop is a free browser extension for primary cardholders with an eligible Citi credit card, including ThankYou points cards and cobranded cards. Citi retail and commercial cards are usually ineligible.

    Offers come as either a percentage back or a fixed amount back, and your earnings are applied as a statement credit on the Citi card you selected during enrollment.

    Citi Shop is separate from Citi Merchant Offers, which requires you to enroll in targeted offers with a specific Citi card and then use that card for the qualifying purchase.

    Both Citi Shop and traditional portals give you an extra reward for making purchases they track.

    It has been revealed that but Citi Shop brings potential rebates to you, rather than requiring you to initiate your savings search. The extension automatically displays a pop-up with an available offer when you visit a participating website. You'll have the option to activate the offer before checkout.

    All of Citi Shop's rebates are provided as statement credits, unlike the potential airline miles, hotel points or credit card rewards of traditional portals.

    What I like about Citi Shop is that it also acts like a shopping assistant. Instead of opening six coupon sites only to discover that every code expired last Tuesday, it handles the scavenger hunt for you and tests available promo codes on your behalf.

    Like Capital One Shopping, Citi Shop uses a browser extension. However, Capital One Shopping doesn't require a Capital One card to enroll and its rewards can be redeemed for eligible gift cards instead of a statement credit.

    Generally speaking, Citi Shop clashes with other shopping portals. Both work by referring and tracking your purchase, so they can be mutually exclusive. You'll need to make your purchase through whichever offer is better.

    Related: Chase shopping portal guide: How to earn bonus Ultimate Rewards points.

    Unless Citi Shop finds a promo code, it won't lower your total at checkout. Its returns arrive later as statement credits and may require patiently waiting two to six months, sometimes longer.

    Even though you need an eligible Citi card to enroll, you don’t have to pay with it. Citi allows any payment method accepted by the merchant.

    Sources indicate that I really appreciate the flexibility to choose the best card for each purchase. For electronics, I might pick a card with an extended warranty while I might stick to a travel rewards credit card for hotel bookings. You can even pay with a gift card if you wish.

    Regardless of how you pay, the statement credit will post to the Citi card you enrolled.

    If you have an eligible Citi card but rarely remember to click through a shopping portal, Citi Shop is an easy win. Install it, activate offers when the pop-up appears and let the credits come to you. That convenience can also be a substantial benefit if you have partners or other family members who aren't as motivated to strategize on rewards as you are.

    It has been revealed that but with a little extra effort, you might be able to earn even more. When the Citi Shop pop-up appears with an offer, take a minute to compare before you click Activate.

    Checking a shopping portal aggregator such as Cashback Monitor indicates payouts from multiple cash-back, airline and credit card portals, making it easier to compare a Citi Shop statement credit with points or miles elsewhere.

    According to recent reports, suppose a $200 jacket is marked down to $160. Citi Shop finds a $10 coupon, bringing the checkout price to $150, and offers 8% back. Assuming the full amount qualifies, you'd receive a $12 Citi Shop credit. If you pay with a card that earns 2% back and has an activated merchant offer for $5 off a $100 purchase, you'd collect another $8. After all the credits and rewards post, your net cost would be $130.

    Read the terms before getting too excited. Some brands, products, gift cards or coupon codes may be excluded and you might not be able to stack every layer every time. Still, you can often use multiple discounts simultaneously for a better deal.

    Sources indicate that citi Shop is not a program for instant gratification. Citi says statement credits post 61 to 180 days after a completed purchase, though some can take longer.

    Recent findings suggest that in many cases, offers may show as pending long before they officially pay out, to account for potential returns. Hotel rewards may remain pending until after the stay. Eventually, you'll see it on your statement as "CITI SHOP STATEMENT CREDIT.".

    Industry observers note that if a credit hasn't posted after the expected window, contact Citi using the number on the back of your enrolled card. You may want to keep good records along the way, like a screenshot of the offer and an e-receipt from the purchase.

    Sources indicate that citi Shop's biggest advantage is convenience. It does the heavy lifting by reminding you to activate offers so you don't miss out on earnings from your online orders, while testing coupon codes along the way. The offers themselves may or may not be the highest available, but they are certainly the easiest.

    In a recent development, to truly optimize your returns, you'll want to compare Citi Shop earnings with those from other shopping portals — and stack other forms of saving along the way. But when that sounds like too much, the ease of this extension can still be a great way to tack on some extra returns.

    #31138. Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited Card Review: Is The $295 Fee Worth It?
