    Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)….

    Sources indicate that with banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail. There’s no denying that consumer preferences have shifted over the years, and along those lines, Amex has just sent an email to card members, informing them that “we’re making the switch to paperless.” Here’s the main part of the email:.

    We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.

    Here’s what happens nextWe want to help you get ready to make the switch too. So, we’ve enrolled your account listed above in the paperless delivery option – but for now, we’ll continue to send you communications about your account in the mail. We’ll also mail your billing statements for the closing dates of November 2026, December 2026, and January 2027.

    After that, we’ll send account communications to you by email, and you’ll receive your monthly billing statements electronically. When they’re ready, you’ll be able to view them anytime by logging in to your account online at americanexpress.com or in the American Express App.

    Recent findings suggest that now, that makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, but I don’t believe that’s actually the case? Because further down in the email, it says this:.

    Recent findings suggest that not ready to go paperless? No problem! You can re-enroll in paper billing statements and account communications by going to americanexpress.com/paperlesssettings, selecting “U.S. Mail,” and following the prompts to opt back in.

    So it seems like what’s happening here is that Amex will try to force everyone into paperless billing by making it the default, but maybe those who specifically once again state their preferences for paper billing will be able to maintain that communication method?

    Suffice it to say that going back 25 years, a vast majority of people got paper statements for their credit cards, while nowadays a vast majority of people get paperless statements, obviously reflecting the shift we’ve seen in how the internet is used.

    In a recent development, it’s funny, because I’m sure 99% of OMAAT readers would be confused at the thought of getting paper bills, and would wonder what purpose that serves. But then there are also people like my dad, who rely on paper statements for their credit cards, pay their statement by phone, etc.

    According to recent reports, so it does sound like people will have the option of opting back into paper billing after being auto-enrolled in paperless billing, so the concept isn’t being eliminated altogether. Still, for my dad, there would likely be quite the learning curve.

    Then again, up until less than a decade ago he didn’t have a cell phone and insisted he didn’t need one, while now he kind of loves it, for everything from texting, to Googling all kinds of stuff. That’s of course a double-edged sword as well, because he seems to believe that if the Google AI summary notes something, it must be true. We’re not talking things like vaccines. Instead, we’re talking things like whether the salmon at Red Lobster is good, etc. Anyway, I digress….

    Recent findings suggest that as of February 2027, Amex will be automatically moving those with paper billing to paperless billing. While the message makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, that doesn’t seem to be the case, as Amex is also telling people they can once again enroll in paper billing statements and account communications if they’re “not ready to go paperless.” So Amex just seems to be trying to thin the ranks here of those using this feature.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-latest business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

    To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet currently consists of 25 planes, including:.

    Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was declared by the tech giant’s CEO at this week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

    The plan is for the 787-9s to get all-newly introduced cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats currently on the planes).

    The 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the first of these Dreamliners will be retrofitted in the next 18 to 24 months (so hopefully by some point in 2028), and then it’ll likely take a couple of years for the fleet to be upgraded.

    Sources indicate that we’ll talk more about the new business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

    Sources indicate that the plane will also have up to 70% more premium seats than before. Right now, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the new premium economy cabin.

    It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

    Recent findings suggest that aeromexico’s new premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

    Recent findings suggest that I imagine that we’ll learn more in the coming months, as this was an unusual way to unveil a newly introduced product. But this does seem to be officially happening, so it’s something to look forward to… down the road.

    Hah: Emirates Puts Auditors On Flights To “Provide Support & Guidance” To Crew

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1160 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, emirates is known for its incredibly high service standards, and that’s largely thanks to the hierarchical system onboard.
    • Recent findings suggest that this system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service problems at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge.
    • Sources indicate that emirates has a rank above pursers, which are the Standard Pursers (which is a weird name, but the idea is that they’re there to audit and enforce “standards”).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, emirates is known for its incredibly high service standards, and that’s largely thanks to the hierarchical system onboard. You have different ranks of flight attendants, then you have supervisors overseeing business class and economy, and then those supervisors report to the purser.

    Recent findings suggest that this system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service problems at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge. Anyway, along those lines, Emirates has just introduced a new initiative, which will no doubt be controversial among flight attendants….

    Sources indicate that emirates has a rank above pursers, which are the Standard Pursers (which is a weird name, but the idea is that they’re there to audit and enforce “standards”). These are specially trained former pursers who no longer work flights in a standard capacity (at least until now), but instead, they audit the crews onboard flights. They have completely different uniforms.

    Emirates’ Chief Operations Officer, Adel Alredha, has just taken to Instagram to highlight a latest initiative involving this small group of employees:.

    On 3 November, Emirates introduced a fresh initiative on select flights, which will have Standard Pursers work alongside cabin crew teams to provide support and guidance to ensure consistently high standards of service.

    This step reflects the airline’s ongoing commitment to maintaining service quality and elevating the customer experience.

    So rather than just auditing the cabins, these Emirates employees will actually be working in the cabin, and that’s sure to ruffle some feathers….

    A post shared by Adel Alredha (@adelalredha).

    Emirates is of course an incredibly global airline with staff from around the world, and I know a thing or two about the internal politics that crews deal with, the different working environments based on who is purser, etc.

    For example, you have some pursers who are incredibly strict to the point that they make their colleagues feel uncomfortable and nervous, while you have other pursers who try to encourage good service by creating a fun environment, etc.

    In a recent development, it goes without saying that historically when a flight had an auditor onboard, everyone would be on their absolute best behavior. In a way that’s no doubt a bit chaotic and stressful, since they’re worried about repercussions if something goes wrong.

    When it comes to this initiative, on the one hand, it’s probably good for these auditors to get some renewed firsthand experience with service, guest expectations, etc. On the other hand, I have to imagine that from the perspective of other crew members, this won’t necessarily be perceived as an effort to “provide support and guidance.”.

    As one commenter on the Instagram post notes, “this is like sending a child to school along with mama with a stick to correct the kid every step.” Another commenter notes “as if there wasn’t already enough pressure on the crew.”.

    I am curious if these flights are still staffed with a regular purser in addition to this special rank of purser, because that could also cause a bit of a butting-of-heads. If an auditor is onboard in their official capacity, it’s clear what everyone’s role onboard is (everyone is there to make sure they perform well!). But if the auditor is there to simply “provide support,” that blurs the lines a little bit, no?

    Anyway, there aren’t actually that many of these auditor pursers at the airline, so presumably only a small percentage of flights will have them. But if you do notice a crew member with a completely different uniform (more silver in color), now you know what’s going on. That would also be a great person to provide any feedback to, because they actually have the ability to get those details to the right person.

    Emirates has Standard Pursers, who are essentially auditors who are assigned select flights, in order to evaluate service from the crew. As of this month, these auditors are also starting to work on flights alongside the crew, to “provide support and guidance.”.

    According to recent reports, there’s no denying that this is an initiative that will make some crew members nervous, since this definitely blurs the line of auditing vs. having an extra set of helping hands. However, given the relatively small number of auditors, they shouldn’t be on too many flights. But if you do see someone in a completely different uniform (other than the standard female purser uniform), then now you know what’s going on.

    What do you make of this Emirates initiative?

    Sources indicate that membership is free and takes no more information than commenting as a guest. Earn status points for good contributions, and see fewer ads as your status grows.

    Your feedback is crucial in helping us keep our community safe.

    The comments on this page have not been provided, reviewed, approved or otherwise endorsed by any advertiser, and it is not an advertiser's responsibility to ensure posts and/or questions are answered.

    Need them on Qatar Airways. Service has not been the same since the war.

    In a recent development, why would an auditor on board create stress? If you are doing what you are supposed to be doing, then there would not be a problem. That auditor that write up how wonderfully well you performed your duties and are ready for promotion.

    Sources indicate that I am a predominantly ground based cabin crew manager for a large European airline but also work as supernumerary crew on 2-3 long haul flights per year. On those flights I wear a uniform and am additional to the crew complement and my role is to support and to a lesser degree assess member of my flying team. I find it really beneficial as airline crew are typically remote workers and rarely have access to their ground manager. It also gives me the ability to see first hand lots of the pain points my team complain to me about - service routines, galley layouts etc. I don't think these kind of roles are that unusual in the airline world. We just aren't called 'Standard Pursers' ouch.

    According to recent reports, if they're not "working" the flight, I could perceive this not going well with customers as well in a way: if you see people constantly passing by you and never checking on you, or if you ask that person for help and they direct it to another person, then it could come across the wrong way. Imagine you press the call attendant button and the Standard Purser just walks right by you. You'd probably think that you're being ignored by staff / they're slacking off.

    If only all airlines had in-flight service auditors, the skies would be a better place.

    According to recent reports, bilt is reportedly seeking to raise $500 million at an $18 billion valuation. That would be roughly two-thirds higher than the $10.75 billion valuation from its last funding round in 2025. They’re asking investors to back a company that wants to influence where people eat, shop, travel and spend their time, starting with the relationship it built through paying rent. Last week Bilt held a dinner for 400 people in the two thousand year old Egyptian Temple of Dendur inside the Metropolitan Museum of Art, with food led by Thomas Keller and Daniel Boulud and a private Jennifer Lopez concert. Ken Chenault, Roger Goodell and Barry Sternlicht were some of the business leaders speaking. The event launched their ‘NeighborhoodOS’ platform. And that provides real insight into the actual Bilt business, where rewards are just one piece of it. Jennifer Lopez’s video from the Met performance Consumers see the side of the business that’s relevant to them. Most people won’t ever view it as anything other than rewards for rent, or a credit card, and that’s fine. The merchant side doesn’t need to understand the travel rewards piece, either. But in case you want a window into what’s really going on, here’s an attempt at an explanation. J. Lo held a private concert at this dinner. I often see remarks on Reddit about how Bilt spends money each month on celebrities hosting its Rent Day, basically seeing that transaction as payment to market Bilt to them (or as just wasted money). That misses half of it. Bilt’s CEO explained the J. Lo relationship, “We agreed to help do the relaunch of her new album.” There’s huge value to the celebrity in being featured in front of Bilt’s audience. The financial terms probably vary with each one, but Bilt gains attention from the celebrity and the celebrity gains access to Bilt’s audience. You often see celebrities with something to promote, like J. Lo’s new album. We naturally see ourselves as the customers being rewarded. Our attention and spending are also what Bilt brings to its partners. That’s how it can negotiate rewards for us. Businesses spend money trying to reach customers, and a rewards program returns some of that money to the people whose business they’re trying to attract. The scale of Bilt’s ambitions are pretty massive. Bilt is trying to eat the world. Or at least a meaningful share of the $6.6 trillion in annual U.S. retail and food services spending it states happens in person. Their business began with a really insightful way to find good customers – reach into their homes, process their rent and get them signed up. Bilt’s latest company announcement says its platform reaches approximately one in four U.S. apartment buildings and expects to process more than $100 billion in housing payments this year. They report more than 8.2 million members and over $12 billion in rewarded spending at local merchants over the past year. Rewarded spending isn’t necessarily spending Bilt caused, but it’s a substantial base of transactions to build their platform off us. As I wrote earlier this year, move-in is a particularly valuable moment. Someone needs a coffee shop, gym, pharmacy and regular place for dinner. Their habits are up for grabs. Acquiring that relationship through their home gives Bilt a chance to influence years of spending. The early audience was especially attractive. In a 2024 interview, its head of loyalty Dave Canty (ex-Starwood, IHG, JetBlue) described core customers aged 24–34, a median age around 29 and average income around $147,000. That made it easier to sign on initial partners who wanted access to the young professionals Bilt was reaching. Airlines start with people who want their miles already sitting on their planes. An independent rewards program has to find its own reason for customers to join. Bilt found one in an expense nearly everyone has, and where there wasn’t competition in offering rewards for their transactions. They offered property owners stickiness as well as a better payment processing platform. American Express’s Plenti had substantial merchants and their customers, but never established a compelling enough new relationship to change spending. It closed in 2018. Coalition rewards have achieved some scale abroad, including Air Miles in Canada and Nectar in Britain. The challenge is making the common program worth choosing over whatever customers already do. Bilt has better tools for that than a small rebate. I consider its points the most valuable transferable currency. A restaurant’s standalone rewards might never accumulate into anything I care about. Combine them with points from housing and other spending, and they can contribute to a Hyatt stay or an international business class award. A restaurant wants nearby customers who spend well and return. It also needs to handle reservations, remember guests, deliver good service and get paid without wasting staff time. Neighborhood OS connects systems the restaurant already uses. OpenTable’s new partnership puts guest information into its table management system and brings personalized offers into the OpenTable app. The restaurant can send an offers to people who’ve just moved nearby and manage offers for regulars – their own loyalty platform. OpenTable reports that participating restaurants have seen: Average checks up to 18% higher among Bilt members than other guests. Table turns reduced by up to 11 minutes on average. Higher average bills may be Bilt’s customer base being higher spending, or they may be encouraging higher spend. That’s not clear. But their technology does seem to speed up paying and leaving, which means serving more guests per table. Bilt’s mobile checkout lets diners tap or scan a receipt card, view the check, split it and pay in a browser. You can leave when you’re finished without waiting for someone to take your credit card and bring it back. Removing dead time after a meal gives the guest back their evening and makes the table available sooner. When there’s demand for another seating, a restaurant can generate more revenue from the same space. Keller and Boulud’s involvement extends beyond preparing food for a launch dinner. In Bilt’s March hospitality announcement, Keller described learning who guests are before they arrive. Boulud talked about inviting wine enthusiasts to wine events and cocktail enthusiasts to cocktail events. Connecting reservations, preferences, past visits and payments helps a restaurant recognize more people than an owner can personally remember. The restaurant can also deliver an experience through other Bilt partners. At Block’s investor day last year, Bilt’s President and Chief Revenue Officer Brandt Smallwood described automating drinks after a third visit, as well as benefits such as dessert or a free Lyft ride at the end of the meal. A ride home can be part of the restaurant’s hospitality, with Bilt doing the work connecting the businesses. The customer doesn’t need to understand the systems behind it. They get recognized, something arrives at their table, and their ride is arranged. That’s different from getting an email with a coupon code to remember next time. There’s also less work for employees. A Google Cloud case study describes Bilt’s concierge moving a reservation and adjusting party size through the underlying systems. It reports about 95% of member conversations handled without a human handoff, up from 86% six months earlier. More partners also means more ways to fund the benefits. Bilt’s acquisition of Banyan brought technology for reading individual items on receipts. A consumer brand can reward the purchase of its product rather than merely knowing someone spent $80 at a store or restaurant. A restaurant supplies a complimentary appetizer, a brand funds a product promotion, a landlord, hotel chain or sports partner funds a member benefit – Bilt connects the offer, the targeted customer and the transaction, and does so in a way no small merchant could accomplish on their own. Constellation Brands is participating, bringing Modelo Especial and Corona Extra benefits to customers across sports fandoms, residential communities, offices and local businesses. A national brand’s marketing budget can help make a neighborhood membership more valuable. An appetizer can cost less to provide than the guest values it. An empty table on Tuesday has different economics from the last table on Saturday. Bilt can help direct incentives to the places and times where they create more business, then show the merchant which offers led to visits and spending. Bilt is also white labeling its membership technology. A sports team can reward fans between games and a hotel program can be useful when a member is home. The organization keeps its customer relationship while Bilt supplies connections to businesses where those customers spend. Some of the expansion is already being bought or distributed through partners: The revealed $300 million LAVA acquisition is supposed to bring relationships with 56 professional sports franchises and more than 300 connections to existing technology systems. Bilt is buying access to audiences and the ability to deliver benefits through ticketing, payments and other systems. Capillary’s planned integration offers a route to clients of an established loyalty provider serving more than 450 brands, including Hertz, Shell and PUMA. Kastle’s partnership would let 60,000 business building access customers offer employee memberships combining office access with neighborhood benefits, like a nearby dry cleaning credit or a team happy hour. Marriott, Hyatt, the Phoenix Suns, Houston Rockets, Houston Texans and Sacramento Kings have been announced as membership partners. Broader integrations roll out starting next year. Verifone, Fiserv, Adyen and OpenTable provide another route into businesses through systems they already use. That gives Bilt distribution on both sides. It can reach consumers through organizations they already belong to and merchants through suppliers they already work with. A competing program would have to assemble enough of both in the same places. And each of these pieces is hard on their own. Bilt earns money from housing and resident technology, merchant commissions, its card business and now additional software subscriptions. Its restaurant pricing is $495 a month for Neighborhood OS plus $195 for Neighborhood Marketplace ($690 combined). Software income from merchant tools gives it another way to make money. I don’t use all their partners but I do use Lyft and Grubhub, and I redeem with Blacklane and BLADE. I book travel through their portal. And their Palladium card is my daily driver. Palladium gets most of my spending and I’ve chosen to preserve 4% Bilt Cash earning. They’ll pry that option from my cold dead hands. (The option offering up to 1.25 points per dollar on housing is what most people choose anyway and still leaves a very good card once 4% back in Bilt Cash goes away for new cardmembers.) Still, my experience isn’t the experience of every member. Bilt told Thrifty Traveler that fewer than 10% of members have its credit card. Someone whose landlord uses Bilt may pay rent through it and do little else. Founder Ankur Jain has called the card “less than 11%” of Bilt’s business (without defining the denominator). That’s not surprising. Delta says roughly one-third of active SkyMiles members carry a cobrand card (without defining ‘active’), while its American Express relationship is on track to generate more than $9 billion this year. But it means that there are also likely a lot of members who don’t transact with Bilt frequently, outside of paying rent. Daily Rewards launches January 15 and looks designed to develop more of that engagement. An on-time housing payment earns a reward with Bilt or a partner, as does one qualifying neighborhood activity per day. Points, Bilt Cash and collectibles toward larger prizes are available. What they’re attempting hasn’t already been done well because it’s hard. Restaurant software is hard. Housing payments are hard. Banking, travel, sports loyalty and customer service are each businesses with their own difficult problems. Putting them together is even more complicated. Jain’s March letter acknowledged that simultaneous integrations, the card transition and mortgage launch strained then and their support suffered. In my experience they ironed out the kinks. They don’t need every category to succeed. There’s a tension for merchants, too: Bilt can make a customer more loyal to a restaurant, but it can also send that customer to the restaurant down the street. The merchant needs enough additional profit to make sharing the customer relationship worthwhile. The scale of ambition here is huge, they’re executing along a lot of different fronts simultaneously. It’s all expensive. If it works, this is – apparently – at least an $18 billion business, holding aside things like liquidation preferences or other undisclosed elements of a financing deal.     Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (939 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks.
    • After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.
    • Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.

    Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.

    The amount of earmarks King secured fell dramatically compared to his previous year's total in Senate Appropriations Committee bills, as Collins took sole credit for most earmarks both senators had requested.

    Recent findings suggest that the power play has instigated a dispute over how to award credit for "congressionally directed spending," better known as earmarks. It has also raised questions about a Senate rule that requires committee leaders to disclose the name of each senator who requested projects to be included in a spending bill before it can move on the floor.

    It’s undeniable that as the chair of the spending panel, Collins has more influence over which projects reach the final bills than her delegation mate. Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller stated that since available earmark funding is split into separate pots for the majority and minority to dole out, the bills reflect which of those funding sources was tapped to provide money to the relevant projects.

    Keller mentioned that Collins deserves sole credit for the contested projects, as listed in the reports accompanying the bills.

    "When only Collins is listed, it reflects only she chose to fund the project,” Keller noted.

    A Democratic committee aide contested that characterization, saying that traditionally all requesters are named regardless of which party’s funding allocation is tapped for a project.

    “The handling of these particular projects is a clear departure from the norm and will need to be rectified in conference negotiations,” the aide said.

    According to recent reports, king is credited with approximately $54 million in fiscal 2027 earmarks in the bills Collins released this month, including joint projects with Collins. That's down from around $231 million in the Senate's fiscal 2026 bills, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis.

    Last year, King and Collins were both listed on 75 of the 77 projects that both requested that were included in the Senate bills, with just two carrying only Collins’ name. This year, Collins claimed sole responsibility for over $125 million in projects that both she and King requested, approximately two-thirds of the joint requests.

    While King’s overall requests fell by more than $200 million this year versus last, his success in securing requested funds plummeted at a far greater rate with less credit for overlapping projects.

    The joint requests for which Collins claimed sole credit include five for the Maine Department of Transportation in the Transportation-HUD bill, including $10.7 million for northern freight rail improvements; $9.6 million for Route 26 reconstruction in Oxford; and $7.2 million for improvements in Rockport, among others.

    In the Labor-HHS-Education bill, projects Collins took sole credit for include $4 million for the University of Maine for biology laboratory equipment and just over $4 million for the creation of a modern emergency helipad at Lincoln Hospital.

    And the Interior-Environment bill features $4 million each for wastewater improvements in Limestone and Kennebec that both Collins and King asked for but are only attributed to Collins, among others.

    Similarly, the Agriculture, Commerce-Justice-Science and Homeland Security bills all include a project requested by both senators that only Collins is listed as securing in the bill.

    The outgoing Appropriations chair’s ability to fuel billions of dollars in federal funding for her state during her career was the centerpiece of her ultimately unsuccessful campaign for reelection, which she lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

    As written, the draft bills appear to risk running afoul of a Senate rule that requires the committee’s chair to identify each senator who requested projects in a bill online at least 48 hours before a vote to advance the legislation on the floor.

    According to recent reports, the relevant rule, Senate Rule 44, states that it is out of order to vote on a motion to proceed to consider a bill unless the chairman of the committee certifies that “each congressionally directed spending item . . . has been identified through lists, charts, or other similar means including the name of each Senator who submitted a request to the committee for each item so identified.”.

    That information must be “available on a publicly accessible congressional website in a searchable format at least 48 hours before such vote.”.

    A King spokesman called on the spending panel to add his name to the relevant requests.

    “We believe this must have been an oversight and assume the committee will revision the requests —per Senate rules — once it’s called to their attention,” King spokesman Matthew Felling remarked.

    The bills released by Collins are drafts, and no floor action on final fiscal 2027 spending bills is expected this Congress. There’s limited time left before the Dec. 11 spending deadline, when all current funding is set to expire, and Democrats want to wait to negotiate final bills until they retake majorities in both chambers next year.

    But to comply with the rule, before the bills reach the floor the reports accompanying the bills, that includes the earmark tables, may have to be rewritten to list King on the contested projects, or the committee may need to disclose the information elsewhere online.

    Both chambers unveiled stricter ethics guidelines surrounding earmarks in 2021 when the practice returned after a decade-long ban.

    Peter Cohn contributed to this report.

    #31110. The American Genius of Madden

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    The American Genius of Madden

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Russell’s Madden, as its story of the Oakland Raiders football coach John Madden shifts between semidocumentary and biopic.
    • Industry observers note that the key to the film’s geniality and surprise is Nicolas Cage’s astounding portrayal of Madden, a former college athlete who blew out his knee but kept his feeling for football.
    • Madden became coach for the Raiders, a team known to play with sheer guts and dedication — qualities the burly Buddha shared with team owner Al Davis (Christian Bale), his wiry, sharklike best friend.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hang on at the start of David O. Russell’s Madden, as its story of the Oakland Raiders football coach John Madden shifts between semidocumentary and biopic. Russell’s uneven, sketchy narrative steadily turns into a probing human comedy. It’s also a slyly monumental tale of American genius found in an Everyman’s commonplace ambition.

    Industry observers note that the key to the film’s geniality and surprise is Nicolas Cage’s astounding portrayal of Madden, a former college athlete who blew out his knee but kept his feeling for football. Cage enters the mindset of a sports fanatic who is also an artist, devising plays and strategies that, considering his size and vision, earn him the nickname “Buddha.” But this is not one of those freak-outs that Cage is known for; he seems to transform himself into John Candy — broad-beamed with a tuft of blond hair and a convincing smile. Cage commits to this genial eccentric who, despite his unreachable idiosyncrasy, is harmless, lovable yet tough — an authentic, original American.

    Madden became coach for the Raiders, a team known to play with sheer guts and dedication — qualities the burly Buddha shared with team owner Al Davis (Christian Bale), his wiry, sharklike best friend. This thick-and-thin Laurel-and-Hardy pair sustain an unlikely partnership. It’s one of the most remarkable depictions of brotherhood in movies — a friendship that persists over temperamental tensions, even after Madden leaves the team and pursues media entrepreneurship to sustain his love of the sport. Madden the broadcaster converts his playbook ingenuity and follows his father’s advice: “Get away with doing what you love for as long as you possibly can.”.

    Sources indicate that russell redeems himself with the oddest-yet-normal collection of American eccentrics. Acting on the edge of parody, Cage and Bale, with their uncanny sincerity, reward Russell’s interest in quirkiness. (Madden hears Davis’s voice in his head.) The fascinating scoundrels of Russell’s terrific American Hustle were preoccupied with manipulating one another. Here, friendship, comradeship, teamwork, and family complications are genuinely recognizable. Scenes that emulate a documentary approach — Madden’s wife Virginia (gung ho comedienne Kathryn Hahn) rivals Jennifer Lawrence’s volatility when speaking directly to the camera — satirize realism to fulfill the non-cynical view of national character that Russell fumbled in the bohemian sojourn of Amsterdam. No wonder De Niro is left out of this particular silver-lined playbook.

    Nicolas Cage (John Madden) in Madden.

    Chuck Zlotnick/Amazon MGM Studios.

    Sources indicate that the patchwork of styles in Madden suggests that Russell investigates American eccentricity as he goes along, finding his way back to the coast-to-coast realness that made his Flirting with Disaster so exhilarating (as in Madden’s surreal, unapologetic pitch for the unique holiday dish the Turducken). Russell adopts Madden’s football-analysis style, such as on-screen telestrator vectors, to humorously examine Madden’s own career shifts and twists of personality (Madden instructing his players, or meeting colleagues Pat Summerall, Howard Cosell, and Bob Costas).

    A dull-witted filmmaker, say James Cameron, would choose an “immersive” style for a movie concerned with the gestalt of football. But Russell’s film is also about the phenomenon of a sport that becomes a vanguard of technology and culture. Madden is pursued by Trip Hawkins (John Mulaney), founder of video game company EA (Electronic Arts), who wants to translate Madden’s football theories for a new generation of at-home fans and gamers. Hawkins’s proposal is scored to Beethoven’s Ninth — another example of Russell’s wit, matching the film’s eclectic score from Barry White and Talking Heads to N.W.A. (“You don’t want to know what that means,” Davis indicates to Madden.).

    Through Madden and Hawkins’s acumen, Russell treats the discovery of a new world as an aftereffect of folk intelligence and ingenuity. Genius is kidded when Hawkins’s team of four-eyed computer nerds demonstrate jock potential after applying Madden’s plays to their algorithms. It’s a sweet way of conveying the phenomenon that would turn EA’s Madden NFL video game franchise into a $4 billion enterprise (some estimates raise that into double digits), with annual compensation going to the Madden family estate.

    More important, Russell (who co-wrote the script with Cambron Clark) sees Madden as a visionary who proudly summarizes TV sportscasting as “They state the obvious, which is f***ing boring.” My only complaint is that Robert Richardson’s photography tends toward frowzy (perhaps deliberately aping TV docs), not as splendid as Oliver Stone’s Any Given Sunday — the greatest football movie ever made.

    In a recent development, madden itself shares biopic sensibility with John Ford’s The Wings of Eagles, respectfully eschewing its subject’s mortality for an optimistic appreciation of a man’s potential. It is unique to American character and the experience of competition and dreams of the NFL Hall of Fame that Madden shared with Al Davis. Russell’s tribute comes complete with a motto: “You make people feel good and alive and good to be American, and I’m not standing in the way of that.” Thus Russell proves his own resilience and the achievement of a new folkloric genre struggling to emerge.

    Armond White is National Review’s culture critic and the author of New Position: The Prince Chronicles and Make Spielberg Great Again: The Steven Spielberg Chronicles.

    On “The American Genius of Madden”.

    Recent findings suggest that A shopping portal generally earns a commission for sending a merchant a sale. Better targeting can make that referral worth more.

    Someone who regularly spends money in a category, but buys from a competitor, is a prospect worth reaching. So is someone who used to shop at a store and stopped. A merchant might pay to bring that person back, get an occasional customer to make another visit, or encourage a larger purchase.

    The best prospect isn’t necessarily the biggest spender. It’s the person whose spending the offer can profitably change. Adidas gains little from paying a committed Adidas customer a huge rebate on shoes they were already going to buy. And it doesn’t much from showing a Nike loyalist an offer they’ll never use.

    Rewards provider Valuedynamx describes a retailer campaign that gave new shoppers stronger incentives, lapsed shoppers offers to bring them back, and loyal customers smaller rewards. Its case study reports a 20.2% incremental sales lift among lapsed customers and 13.3% among new ones.

    Targeting also lets a brand offer a substantial rebate without cutting the public price for everyone. It can spend more to win a customer it wants while avoiding an expensive storewide sale.

    Why Aerolíneas Argentinas Is Basically An Ultra Low Cost Carrier In Disguise

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.
    • As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.
    • However, I quickly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.

    As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.

    However, I quickly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.

    According to recent reports, I needed to get from Buenos Aires to Mendoza for a friend’s 40th birthday celebrations. Options were pretty limited, with nonstop flights available with either JetSmart or, indeed, Aerolíneas Argentinas. I try to avoid low-cost airlines when possible, because, quite simply, I enjoy the flying experience, and low-cost airlines tend to suck every enjoyable element out of it.

    Other pros to booking Aerolíneas Argentinas, personally:.

    After researching my options, I used Flying Blue miles to book two single tickets from Buenos Aires Jorge Newbery Aeroparque Airport (AEP) to Mendoza’s El Plumerillo Airport (MDZ).

    I can’t remember how much the fares were when I was planning the trip, but each one-way flight cost a total of 7,500 miles and less than $10 in taxes and fees.

    Looking now at example fares for January next year, round-trips for Aerolíneas’ lowest and most restrictive fare category (more on that to come) start at around $120.

    I know it’s not a hard-and-fast rule, but I’ve come to expect that, most of the time, the baggage allowance listed on the booking confirmation is correct. This is often true with redemptions, such as British Airways, which notably offers and acknowledges a 23 kg baggage allowance when redeeming Avios, even for a short-haul flight in economy.

    The confirmation email I received clearly noted 1x checked bag with a 23 kg limit.

    Again, the attached PDF stated that I’d have 1x checked bag included.

    Industry observers note that as the Argentinian scamsters would have it, I learned at check-in that the airline has a 15 kg weight limit for checked bags on domestic flights. I tried to plead my case and indicated the rather unhelpful check-in agent my booking confirmation, but he basically said, “that means nothing.”.

    So they weigh your bag, give you a ticket, and then you have to exit the terminal building and find this little cashier where they collect their scammy little earnings. And what better place to proudly display a “SkyTeam Alliance Member” sign at the very desk where the airline also proudly collects baggage fees from SkyTeam elite status holders, even when traveling on award tickets?

    In a recent development, once I’d been charged the fee of around $17, I had to join another queue back inside and show them I’d paid for the extra weight before they’d dispatch my bag. You might look at the $32 in fees I paid and think, “What is he complaining about?” But this isn’t about the actual amount of money; it’s the principle.

    Only after the debacle did I learn the extent of Aerolíneas Argentinas’ domestic fare restrictions. Imagine paying $510 (more than four times the cheapest fare) for a “premium economy” ticket and still only getting 15 kg checked baggage allowance, no Fast Pass, no priority boarding (what?), and no lounge access. The latter isn’t such a significant deal as Aerolíneas Argentinas doesn’t even have its own lounge at AEP.

    Airline loyalty is really important to me, and I generally value it more than the ability to redeem miles. Maybe I’ll get into that another day….

    Things got off to a fairly normal start when I saw the Sky Priority check-in kiosks at Aeroparque.

    Industry observers note that that feeling of normalcy lasted as long as it took me to get from the sign to the aforementioned conversation about the checked bag situation at the desk. Despite my very best efforts combining my Castilian Spanish and Geordie charm (we’re called Geordies where I’m from in the North East of England), the man at the check-in desk seemed to take real pleasure in explaining that the checked bag rules on my booking confirmation were irrelevant and I’d have to pay the fee.

    For what it’s worth, Sky Priority check-in was also available at Mendoza.

    Being nickel-and-dimed for a checked bag by a flag carrier airline is shameful.

    Back at Aeroparque, there was no fast track, and the security line was ridiculously long. That mentioned, it’s rare in South America to have fast track lanes. For example, no matter whether you’re flying economy or first class (even Air France La Première), everyone waits in the same line to clear pre-departure passport control at São Paulo’s Guarulhos.

    Thanks to my Priority Pass, I did have access to the surprisingly nice AMAE lounge in the national departures part of the airport.

    Even from the outside, my 15-year-old Embraer 190 looked like it had seen better days. The zebra-striped dirt streaks running from each window suggested this place hadn’t been washed or hit the maintenance hangar for a while.

    Inside the Embraer, however, could have been a lot worse. The older seats had thick padding, and despite being a small 2-2-configured cabin, it felt bright and spacious.

    It was the Uber advertising on every single headrest that I found most jarring.

    Sources indicate that the legroom was decent, too. The retro seatback screens, on the other hand, were pretty much redundant.

    It was stepping on board the 16-year-old Boeing 737-700 back to Buenos Aires that Aerolíneas Argentinas’ low-costness was most glaring. Looking at this, I would never guess this plane belonged to a flag carrier. The seats were very uncomfortable, and I think I remember they didn’t recline either.

    According to recent reports, as for service, I don’t recall it being particularly good or particularly bad. Forgettable is probably the most accurate word.

    Imagine the likes of Spirit (RIP) or Ryanair calling itself a national flag carrier; that’s basically what Aerolíneas Argentinas is. I’m planning a trip with my dad and brother for February next year that includes Argentina, and I will actively avoid flying Aerolíneas, even if it means forgoing the chance to earn any Flying Blue miles and XPs.

    It’s almost as if the airline has been abandoned. After all, the only real competition is low-cost airlines at LATAM — the full-service carrier which dominates South America. Who knows, maybe things will change come 2028 when it takes delivery of new Airbus A330-900s and Boeing 737 MAXs.

    If I were a power that be at SkyTeam, I’d definitely remove the airline from the alliance. And if I had my way, Aerolíneas Argentinas would be bought by LATAM, and the cherry on top would be LATAM joining SkyTeam. I should probably put a business case together for that….

    Sources indicate that I flew from GRU to LHR on BA in about 2018, first class redemption. I don't remember a long passport queue, but I do remember that I was escorted by the check-in agent from the desk to the lounge which I found surprising, but could explain the lack of concerns. Have the rules changed, or have air France not worked out how to bypass the queue?

    LATAM is no better. I had to fight tooth and nail with them at AEP over baggage allowances. I finally got a stupervisor and quoted actual tariff rules. She was a bit shocked and rapidly backed off. Average Joe would not have not known what they were trying to pull. LATAM is just another ULCC that happens to fly international.

    In a recent development, @Daniel--Welcome to OMAAT. I can understand your disappointment with AR. We value loyalty program status for what it takes to achieve it as well as its promised benefits. When those benefits are not delivered, one has a right to complain. However, I agree that your complaint likely should be with the FlyingBlue program, which issued your ticket. I haven't been to Argentina recently but years ago, I liked how convenient AEP was as compared to EZE, at least for domestic flights. Sorry to hear that the security lines are so long. My most recent foray into South America was to Chile, where I flew 4 domestic segments on LAN as a SkyTeam Elite+ member. All of the expected elite benefits were available to me and a companion on the same itineraries, i.e., I had none of the issues you described. So, your characterization of AR may be correct.

    Hi Daniel! Great review but I’m afraid I might have to disagree a little with you here based on my personal experiences with AR this April and November. It is a shame that FB sent you an email that conflicted with AR’s policy. I suspect that it might be FB’s fault and not AR because it’s a standard email template. I flew with AR 4 times this year both domestically within Argentina and internationally. Their unconventional luggage allowance was stated quite clearly at online check-in. Unless you did not check in online or missed it ;). As for the checked luggage allowance in practice, I’ve found that it’s a YMMV situation. On 3 of my 4 legs with AR this year, the check-in agents accepted all the bags that I had paid for and the cabin bags that I had not. On my fourth leg AEP-IGR about two weeks ago (early Nov 2026), the agent told me that I had exceeded my allowance by one entire piece that weighed 8kg, which was unfortunate but fair. I had to pay the fee outside and it came up to US$10. Unlike you however, I did not have to go back in to show my EMD as proof of payment. It was automatically dispatched. I had some time at AEP and a chatty agent with whom I could practice my imperfect Argentine Spanish. She clarified with a few shrugs that there is no clear formula for calculating the fee. It seems to be a combination of fare class, date of booking mixed in with some Argentine chaos and charm. The maintenance problems, delays and their handling of irregular ops are two other stories altogether though.

    Glad to always hear more about AR, even if it is not always positive news, and welcome to the blog ^^.

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A Southwest Airlines passenger indicates she was settled into an exit row window seat in Las Vegas, pleased about the empty middle seat beside her, when the crew began looking for her husband.
    • Industry observers note that angie Batis states she offered to buy her own ticket, using a credit card or points, but was told it was too late.
    • She’d spent four days in Las Vegas, checked two 50 pound bags, and was ready to get home.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A Southwest Airlines passenger indicates she was settled into an exit row window seat in Las Vegas, pleased about the empty middle seat beside her, when the crew began looking for her husband. He wasn’t coming—and she was traveling on his Companion Pass. Angie Batis says she offered to buy her own ticket, using a credit card or points, but was told it was too late. Instead, she was escorted off the roughly 9 p.m. flight to Boise and quoted about $400 for a departure the next morning. Southwest was right about the Companion Pass rule. Surely though it shouldn’t take materially longer to sell a ticket than to remove a passenger. She’d spent four days in Las Vegas, checked two 50 pound bags, and was ready to get home. Sitting in row 14, she’d already given the flight attendant her verbal agreement to help with the emergency exit. Her headphones were on. She was listening to an audiobook and playing a game on her phone. Then came the announcement asking Mr. Batis to identify himself. She told the crew he wasn’t on board and wouldn’t be joining them. That’s when she realized why the middle seat was empty. An employee came back to her row and explained that her free ticket depended on her husband actually taking the flight. Well, can I just pay with a credit card? … I’ve been a Southwest card member for 20 plus years. I have my own points. Can I just book it, you know, pay for it now? She says he told her they were ready to push back. He left, returned about three minutes later, and told her she’d have to get off. She gathered her things and went with him. I think he was expecting, like, some complete chaos. @angiebatis — Her account of being removed from the Southwest flight Companion Pass Requires The Passholder To Travel I’ve been a Companion Pass holder, including through promotions, and it’s still an extraordinary deal. Book your own Southwest flight with money or points, then add your designated companion for taxes and fees starting at $5.60 each way, as long as there’s a seat available. The free travel is tied to accompanying the passholder. Her husband paid for a ticket, which then supports the companion’s ticket. The rules though are very clear: If the Companion is not traveling with the Member, the Companion’s reservation will be canceled. I’ve covered almost this exact situation before. In June 2024, a companion boarded Southwest flight 2097 from Savannah to Baltimore. The passholder canceled his own ticket just before departure. Southwest removed the companion, conducting a manual boarding pass check to find her in the days before assigned seating. That case involved a cancellation and an apparent attempt to get the companion transported while refunding the underlying ticket. Here the passenger was fully willing to pay. I don’t think she was actually trying to scam the airline, though she’d be traveling free (and if her husband did cancel in time prior to departure he’d still have his flight credit to use). The requirement to fly together isn’t one of the changes Southwest is making to Companion Pass in 2027. It’s been a longstanding requirement. She Offered To Pay For The Seat Comments on the woman’s video between people who think a longtime Southwest customer should know how the pass works and people who think the airline should have found a way to get her home. It’s probably just best that she got off without making a scene. Several viewers ask why this wasn’t caught at check-in or at the gate. But checking in isn’t the same as boarding. If her husband wasn’t checked in though it should get caught at the check-in deadline. He may have been checked in and just didn’t board. There’s an interesting bit of history here. This same woman went viral in 2024 praising a Southwest gate agent in Phoenix. She filmed herself thanking an employee named Krista for her kindness. In this video, she also thanks the gate agent and tells her it isn’t her fault. Her host at the Venetian arranged a chauffeur, another room, dinner and a car back to the airport. She was still separated from her checked bags, without a phone charging cord or a brush. I bet her casino host could manage that… So this was day old hair yesterday. Today it’s two day old hair. …I was embarrassed, I was humiliated, I was mad at my husband, the whole thing.     End Of An Era: American Retires Boeing 777 Flagship First Class

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (904 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore.
    • As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.
    • Specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore. The good news is that an updated business class product is in the process of being rolled out, and that’s something that should benefit a lot of travelers.

    As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.

    Specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet. As of this week, the airline is no longer selling first class on these planes. Now, plenty of 777-300ERs with these cabins are still flying around, as American has just started reconfiguring its 777-300ERs with newly introduced cabins, including the new business class.

    Sources indicate that still, for flights effective immediately, first class seats are just being sold as standard business class seats, and any business class passenger can select seats in the first two rows (you’d think they’d try to charge extra or at least reserve them for select elite members, but nope). So there will no longer be a differentiated soft product… not that there was much of a difference as of late anyway!

    According to recent reports, with this change, no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore either, so it very much is the end of an era. American’s 777 first class seats were controversial — on the one hand, I kind of love how they swivel, though on the other hand, they really lack privacy, and the soft product left a lot to be desired.

    I expect we’ll continue to see these planes flying around well into late 2027, or possibly even into 2028, depending on how fast the retrofit project happens. American’s dedicated first class ground product has also largely been discontinued, as Flagship First Dining has turned into Flagship Dining, so a la carte lounge dining is now available to eligible business class passengers as well.

    It’s great that these planes will be getting new business class suites, as they’ll also be the aircraft belonging to a US carrier with the most business class seats, as they’ll have 70 of them… that’s lot!

    While American has now eliminated its international first class product, it’s worth emphasizing that the airline still technically has a “premium” first class, in the sense of a cabin above business class.

    In a recent development, specifically, American still has its specially configured Airbus A321T aircraft, which are used primarily for flights between New York (JFK) and Los Angeles (LAX) and San Francisco (SFO). The planes have 10 reverse herringbone seats spread across five rows, in a 1-1 configuration.

    American also plans to eliminate this product, as the A321Ts will be reconfigured into standard A321 domestic configuration aircraft, and A321XLRs will be taking over the transcon routes.

    American has stopped selling first class on these planes for flights as of March 28, 2027. After that date we’ll still see some of the planes flying with the cabins, but the first class seats will simply be sold as business class.

    American Airlines has officially eliminated its international first class product, as Boeing 777-300ERs no longer have Flagship First for sale. These planes are being retrofitted, as first class seats are being eliminated, and new business class suites are being introduced. However, the planes will keep flying around with the current cabins for quite some time, and business class passengers can freely assign the first class seats.

    In the spring, we’ll see American eliminate its last “premium” first class product, which is the A321T first class cabin, as those planes are replaced by A321XLRs.

    What do you make of the end of American’s Flagship First on the 777?

    House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1331 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, indicates banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take.
    • After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.
    • But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the issue could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, indicates banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.

    But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the issue could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.

    According to recent reports, “I’d rather have it be a clean bill focused on stock trading, and not muddy it by adding other topics, even if they’re good policies,” stated Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I.

    Industry observers note that the incoming majority could plant a flag on government accountability with a broad package ranging from insider trading to campaign finance and more. Or they could zoom in on the stocks issue with a standalone bill.

    Magaziner said he hasn’t received any assurances from House Democratic leaders, instead describing a “collaborative conversation” about what form the legislation could take.

    “I worry that it would get weighed down under its own weight if you try to load it up with too many things,” Magaziner noted, while stressing he would support whatever expected incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries decides.

    Meanwhile, more than half of the Democrats in the incoming freshman class are calling for action on Day One of the new Congress, sending a letter to Jeffries last week suggesting they make a “down payment on much-needed reform” by changing House rules to curb stock trading.

    “Democrats may have won the election, but we have a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country,” reads the letter, led by Reps.-elect Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa and Jamie Ager of North Carolina. “A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them.”.

    Industry observers note that folding fresh language into the House’s internal rules would be a relatively easy path, requiring just a majority vote on the House floor, instead of passage in both chambers and the president’s signature. But such internal limits wouldn’t have the force of law, and some believe it would cool the urgency around the issue while doing little to crack down on insider trading.

    Colorado Rep. Jason Crow remarked moving forward swiftly with a rule change wouldn’t preclude passing a bill, suggesting his fellow Democrats do both.

    “I want to pursue a parallel track,” said Crow, who co-chairs the End Corruption Caucus. “We want to move via rule and just prohibit it right out of the gate, or as much as we can.”.

    Jeffries has repeatedly said the topic is high on his to-do list as he looks to deliver on the accountability the “American people are demanding.”.

    Sources indicate that “We’re committed to making sure we pass legislation that bans members of Congress from trading stocks. That will be a high priority,” he noted at a news conference this week.

    But with more than two dozen different bills on the topic introduced over the past few years alone, lawmakers will have to decide exactly what a “ban” means to them.

    Some want to force members of Congress to fully offload their stocks with the exception of widely held mutual funds. Other proposals would block lawmakers from buying newly introduced stocks but allow them to keep the ones they already own, like a Republican-led bill that passed the House earlier this year but stalled in the Senate.

    Democrats resisted that push, which was led by outgoing House Administration Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., partly because it included an unrelated voter ID provision they called a “poison pill.” Many also complained the measure didn’t go far enough, extending to members’ spouses and dependent children but leaving out key figures in other branches of government, such as the president.

    In a recent development, rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., stated she wants to stay close to the text of a consensus bill she hammered out last year with a small bipartisan group that included Magaziner and Reps. Chip Roy, R-Texas, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa.

    “That is the most comprehensive, thorough, thoughtful proposal and bipartisan proposal that we have,” she remarked of the bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Congress Act.

    According to recent reports, that measure would not apply to President Donald Trump, as many Democrats have urged as they seek to draw attention to his ballooning wealth while in office. Still, Jayapal suggested a presidential stock trading ban could be moved separately.

    It has been revealed that “There is discussion about the president, vice president, Cabinet, Supreme Court. I know we’re working on some language around enforcement, around those pieces, but I actually think that can be a separate bill,” Jayapal said. “We want to hold everyone accountable — but at minimum, we have to do ourselves.”.

    It’s not clear how much appetite will exist next year for a bipartisan compromise that could realistically clear a 60-vote cloture threshold in the Senate. Notably, key Republicans who worked on the consensus bill will be leaving Congress, with Roy losing a primary bid for Texas attorney general and Fitzpatrick unseated by a Democratic challenger.

    While lawmakers could in theory advance a latest stock-trading bill even sooner, before Democrats take control of both chambers, time and patience is short in the lame-duck session.

    At a news conference at the Capitol earlier this week with Crow and Jayapal, a group of freshman and returning Democrats took matters into their own hands, promising not to hold or trade individual stocks as part of a broader pledge backed by the Political Integrity Project.

    “My district, Newly introduced York 10, happens to include Wall Street, but I don’t represent Wall Street. I represent the people of Brooklyn and Manhattan who deserve someone who goes to work every single day and shows right up front, ‘I work for you.’ And what better way to prove that than by day one showing we will ban members of Congress from enriching themselves, from trading stocks?” Rep.-elect Brad Lander stated.

    According to recent reports, while momentum has grown in recent years as key senior lawmakers softened their resistance to a stock trading bill, not everyone is on board. Some members still argue, whether publicly or privately, that they should be able to trade on the stock market just like other citizens or that existing disclosure requirements established by a 2012 law are already enough to discourage dubious trades.

    Industry observers note that as they iron out the legislative text of any fresh bill, members will have to decide how to handle emerging topics such as prediction markets and crypto, along with sticky questions such as whether to allow blind trusts. And extending restrictions to the president could be a nonstarter for many Republicans.

    Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said Democrats in the next Congress should look to a bipartisan bill that advanced out of the Senate Homeland and Governmental Affairs Committee in July 2025 as a model.

    In a recent development, “The legislation we passed out of the committee applied to the executive branch,” he stated. “But it didn’t take effect for anybody until their next terms, which was a compromise.”.

    Recent findings suggest that that proposal would apply to future presidents but not the current one, potentially freeing up more Republicans to vote for it without angering Trump. Still, it hasn’t seen action on the Senate floor.

    Hawley said that while he’d like to see a “full ban on trading and holding” in Congress, he would be open to a weaker proposal in the interest of getting something done.

    “I’ll take anything that’s an incremental improvement over what we have now, which is nothing,” he said.

    Aris Folley contributed to this report.

    According to recent reports, we’ve just seen American formally retire its Boeing 777 first class, and with that, no airline in the United States has a “true” international first class anymore. It’s the end of an era, because going back many decades, premium products were largely pioneered by US carriers. So I think this raises the question — why can US carriers not make first class work in a way that’s economically viable, especially as they keep talking about how premium they are?

So how is it that carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, SWISS, etc., can make money offering first class to the United States (primarily targeting Americans), but US airlines seemingly can’t?

    The US has way too many people with tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, or even billions of dollars. There are plenty of people who would pay to fly private, and would pay for Air France La Premiere first class, but would never consider paying the high price for first class on a US carrier, because it’s just not worth it.

    When they fly first class, they want this….

In other words, first class has long been thought of as “upgrade class,” rather than something actually worth paying for. US carriers have managed to change that narrative on domestic flights, but not so much on international flights.

    Recent findings suggest that in terms of economics, let me also point out that the opportunity cost of a first class cabin isn’t actually that high. “Premium” is all the rage, so what you do here is eliminate some economy seats:.

    Industry observers note that at this point, no airline from the United States offers first class on international flights anymore. For airlines that can’t stop talking about how unbelievably premium they are, I find that to be a pretty perplexing reality. I know that many people have just accepted “oh, a good business class is the future,” but I have a different take.

The concern is, US carriers have long not actually given people a reason to fly first class, all while offering too much capacity.

    ⏱️ ~50 mins left to finish
