    #30987. Tech Report: China’s AI Diplomacy Is Working

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2487 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: China’s AI Diplomacy Is Working

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2487 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that DANIEL REMLER is a Senior Fellow with the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a Latest American Security.
    • Can the United States and China simultaneously cooperate and compete on AI?
    • Beijing has long appreciated this dynamic.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that DANIEL REMLER is a Senior Fellow with the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a Latest American Security. He served as AI Policy Coordinator in the Office of the Special Envoy for Critical and Emerging Technology at the State Department from 2023 to 2025.

    And America Should Be Taking Notes.

    Can the United States and China simultaneously cooperate and compete on AI? That is the question driving debates in Washington about the wisdom of pursuing talks on the subject with Beijing. The Biden administration paired sweeping technology restrictions with a narrow dialogue on risk, and the Trump administration has kept a channel open even as it has downplayed safety. Some experts go further. They hope that cooperation on safety can be siloed off from competition entirely, a belief as appealing as it is fanciful. Any dialogue on AI risk takes place within the broader strategic competition between the United States and China.

    Beijing has long appreciated this dynamic. Much of Washington has not. Whereas the United States has shifted its approach to AI competition and safety across and within presidential administrations, Beijing has kept its AI diplomacy focused on gaining competitive advantage over the United States. China has taken part in international AI safety discussions, but it has used them, along with talks with the United States, to paint U.S. export controls as the main obstacle to cooperation. It has cast itself as the champion of the developing world, promising a Chinese-led AI ecosystem without technological or financial barriers as an alternative to a restrictive U.S.-led AI order. The pitch is working. A growing number of states are embracing China’s message, and Chinese open-weight models are gaining owners across the developing world.

    According to recent reports, if the United States wants to maintain its lead and make meaningful progress on safety, it needs to treat the dialogue as part of the competition with China. To do so, it must ramp up pressure on China outside the talks and offer countries still choosing sides a more compelling vision for AI adoption and governance. And when U.S. and Chinese officials next meet, in November, Washington should test Beijing’s seriousness about safety. In short, the United States should approach AI diplomacy with the same strategic clarity China has.

    It has been revealed that the Biden administration’s first round of advanced semiconductor export controls in October 2022 and the release of ChatGPT a month later signaled that the United States had taken an early lead in the AI competition and would act to weaken China’s AI industry. Washington and its allies also seized the diplomatic initiative, taking the first steps toward global AI governance. In May 2023, the G-7 began intense discussions on AI governance that would eventually produce a code of conduct for developers. Weeks later, the United Kingdom announced it would host the first global AI safety summit at Bletchley Park.

    Recent findings suggest that china responded by rolling out a diplomatic script it has been honing ever since. Its core tenets first appeared in the Global AI Governance Initiative, published in October 2023. It called for countries to “put equal emphasis on development and security” (though it left security to be defined by individual states) and contrasted China’s focus on cooperation and development with U.S. export controls, attacking Washington for “creating barriers and disrupting the global AI supply chain through technological monopolies and unilateral coercive measures.” Despite Beijing’s growing body of AI regulations at home, the initiative offered little more than slogans on the technology’s risks.

    It has been revealed that that basic formula—cooperation and development, set against U.S. restrictions, with little to say about risk—has guided China’s AI diplomacy for the last three years. In March 2024, the UN General Assembly adopted a U.S.-led resolution on safe, secure, and trustworthy AI intended to appeal to both developed and developing countries. China supported the resolution, then introduced another resolution centered on help for poorer countries and “emphasizing that member states should enjoy equal opportunities” to develop and use AI. At a UN Security Council meeting on AI chaired by the United States in December that year, China’s UN ambassador, Fu Cong, once again counterposed Beijing’s stated interest in cooperation against “discriminatory barriers based on ideological differences.” In thinly veiled terms, Fu was charging that U.S. restrictions on China harmed the developing world.

    In a recent development, to win the support of these countries as they built out their AI infrastructure, China needed a bloc of its own. In July 2025, Premier Li Qiang proposed the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), which promised developing countries technology, training, and a greater say in writing global AI rules. In a speech marking its launch a year later, Chinese leader Xi Jinping called for “openness,” shorthand for access to U.S. chips and the adoption of Chinese open-weight models. After urging countries to take the risks of AI seriously, Xi added that they should, “in the meantime,” jointly oppose “overstretching the national security concept in the field of AI and placing one country’s security over that of others.” Cooperation on risks, in Xi’s telling, was subordinate to overcoming U.S. restrictions.

    WAICO has rapidly gained standing among its target audience. An early endorsement by UN Secretary-General António Guterres lent it immediate credibility in the eyes of developing countries, and Chinese officials have since promoted WAICO in frequent speeches and in bilateral meetings with countries as varied as Brazil, Pakistan, and Serbia. Beijing has signaled that membership will come with perks. Its draft export controls on leading models, released in October, promise to help WAICO’s 37 members build their AI capabilities, suggesting members could have easier access to models restricted for the rest of the world.

    Industry observers note that xi personally led this diplomatic offensive in the lead-up to the Washington summit with U.S. President Donald Trump in September. During a speech in Kyrgyzstan, he pledged to expand a Chinese AI center for the Shanghai Cooperation Organization that helps members build local language models and train engineers. In Cairo, he and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi signed agreements on AI, data centers, and semiconductors, which have become a staple of Xi’s trips abroad. And in New Delhi, Xi proposed an open-source AI zone for BRICS members and told other leaders that a “small yard, high fences” approach would only “box oneself in and divide the world.” AI risks were nowhere on the agenda. The message instead was that U.S. restrictions would isolate Washington, not Beijing.

    Much of the allure of China’s pitch rests on how the country’s developers share their technology. Chinese developers release their best models with open weights, which any government or company can download, run on its own hardware, and adapt to its own language. For governments wary of depending on American companies whose exports Washington can restrict, open-weight models promise a greater degree of control. Chinese developers rarely conduct or publish the results of any safety testing for these models, leaving others to discover after release whether, for example, they can be used to launch cyberattacks or build weapons. But their accessibility allows Beijing to argue that any effort to contain the risks of Chinese models is an attempt to deny AI to the developing world.

    Sources indicate that china’s approach to bilateral AI talks with the United States has deflected discussions of risk just as assiduously as its global AI diplomacy has. In May 2024, the United States and China held talks in Geneva, which I joined as part of the U.S. delegation. The U.S. objective of the talks was to test whether an in-depth technical exchange with China on AI risk was possible. The answer was no. Chinese diplomats steered the discussion away from risks for hours and declined to even explain China’s own AI regulations beyond a superficial overview, despite having technical experts from the relevant agencies in the room.

    In a recent development, the Chinese position came through most clearly in the opening and closing remarks of the delegation’s most senior officials. They began with an appeal for cooperation on capacity-building projects in the developing world. They then cast U.S. technology restrictions as an attempt to contain China’s development and the U.S. emphasis on safety as a barrier preventing developing countries from accessing and using AI. The implication was clear—export controls were the primary impediment to cooperation on AI safety. The one concrete outcome, a November 2024 statement in which former President Joe Biden and Xi affirmed “the need to maintain human control over the decision to use nuclear weapons,” asked little of Beijing.

    According to recent reports, this September, after the summit between Trump and Xi in Washington, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs published an “eight-point consensus,” Beijing’s account of what the two sides had agreed to. It described the dialogue as an exchange on the “risks and benefits” of AI. But whereas the White House framed the dialogue as a security problem, listing it alongside nuclear arms control, China’s Ministry of Commerce stressed instead that talks had taken place, and would continue, under the two countries’ economic and trade mechanism. Folded into trade talks, a dialogue on AI risks and benefits leaves Beijing free to parry U.S. requests on risks, such as limits on openly releasing models with dangerous capabilities, by demanding that Washington relax export controls.

    Xi did propose to “jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI,” conveniently eliding China’s own frequent use of AI against the United States in various ways, such as hacking campaigns and influence operations. He added that AI should remain under human control and be developed for good, a principle Beijing has repeated since 2023 but about which it has offered little further detail or follow-through. More pointed was his insistence that future dialogue should “draw on each other’s strengths, not guard against each other” and his request that Chinese companies be “treated fairly,” both implicit rebukes of U.S. restrictions.

    In a recent development, this record suggests Beijing will come to future meetings, beginning with the next discussion in November, with proposals designed to put Washington in a bind. Although U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has made clear that export controls are not on the table, Beijing will raise them anyway. If Washington engages, Chinese negotiators will claim a standing channel where U.S. restrictions on AI technology are up for negotiation. If it refuses, Beijing will continue to evade U.S. entreaties on safety while accusing Washington of stifling opportunity for developing countries. It hopes that every round of the dialogue will further cement an impression among allies such as Japan and the Netherlands that Washington will trade away restrictions over their heads, and that they should accommodate China’s AI ambitions, too.

    But Washington is in a stronger position than its diplomacy has let on. The world’s leading models are still American, and, together with allies, the United States controls key chokepoints in the semiconductor supply chain. Export controls on those chokepoints are not a bargaining chip and should be strengthened. Chinese AI companies regularly lament their lack of high-end chips and have resorted to smuggling chips and illicitly distilling U.S. models. U.S. developers also conduct increasingly extensive and transparent safety testing, which Chinese developers avoid. Taken together, these strengths give Washington the means to press Beijing and an attractive offer for the rest of the world. It should use them, advertising its rigorously tested models to compete for global adoption while pressuring China on safety in the dialogue.

    According to recent reports, the first chance to apply that pressure is the next bilateral meeting. Washington should set two conditions for it and future meetings. Chinese developers must commit to publishing safety evaluations at least as extensive as those that leading U.S. developers publish today on equivalent benchmarks for the most serious risks, such as cyberattacks and biological weapons, and to disclosing previous and future incidents. The United States can make the same commitments, as its companies already publish such evaluations, increasingly disclose incidents, and open their models to independent and government evaluators before release. Otherwise, the incident channel to which the two sides agreed in September will run one way, with China free to point to U.S. incidents while reporting none of its own.

    Sources indicate that these conditions would change the terms of the dialogue. Since 2023, Washington has raised risks and Beijing has steered the conversation toward development. As long as Chinese companies face no scrutiny for the risks of their models, Beijing can tout them for their openness and innovation without having to answer questions from the rest of the world about their safety. Concordia AI, which tracks China’s AI ecosystem, found that only five of China’s ten leading developers published safety test results for any model over the past year, and none did so consistently. If China agrees, governments and companies choosing which models to use will be able to judge Chinese and American developers by the same criteria. If China refuses, the onus will be on Beijing to explain why fair treatment for Chinese companies should not extend to safety testing. Regardless, the U.S. government should ramp up its own tests of latest Chinese models and publish the results. It should also avoid unforced errors, such as Trump’s waving away of AI safety concerns as a “hoax,” which hand Beijing an easy retort to U.S. appeals.

    Industry observers note that more broadly, effective AI diplomacy ultimately requires convincing other countries to join the American AI ecosystem. Countries that train their engineers, build their local language models, and run their data centers on Chinese technology will come to depend on it. To counter that dependence (and prevent it from turning into political alignment), Washington needs to present a positive vision of AI governance that pairs verifiable safety commitments—the kind Chinese developers avoid—with the access and investment developing countries want.

    U.S. companies already offer the best technology, but Washington has yet to put real diplomatic weight behind them. It should draw from its evolving approach at home to rally partners around shared safety measures. Under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed in September, six leading U.S. companies committed themselves to internal controls, external audits, and independent oversight. The G-7 Code of Conduct, which built on voluntary commitments secured under the Biden administration, could incorporate the accord’s measures and serve as a common standard for partners. Countries that agree to its measures could receive priority for technology and financing. Without such incentives, the AI competition may be determined by price and access alone, where China has the edge.

    Much of Washington has treated talks with Beijing as a place to manage the shared risks of AI apart from the competition. China has always treated them as an arena of the larger rivalry. To maintain its lead and make real progress on safety, the United States should start doing the same.

    Why Did Trump Attend ASEAN?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The highlights this week from the ASEAN summit in Manila, Philippines: Trump stops by for 24 hours; Myanmar is still shut out despite junta lobbying; and Canada forges two upcoming trade deals in the region.
    • The highlights this week from the ASEAN summit in Manila, Philippines: Trump stops by for 24 hours; Myanmar is still shut out despite junta lobbying; and Canada forges two new trade deals in the region.
    • So keen was the Philippines to have U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

    The highlights this week from the ASEAN summit in Manila, Philippines: Trump stops by for 24 hours; Myanmar is still shut out despite junta lobbying; and Canada forges two upcoming trade deals in the region.

    Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

    The highlights this week from the ASEAN summit in Manila, Philippines: Trump stops by for 24 hours; Myanmar is still shut out despite junta lobbying; and Canada forges two new trade deals in the region.

    So keen was the Philippines to have U.S. President Donald Trump attend the annual leader’s summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) that it changed the dates just for him. Originally scheduled to run five days earlier, it was shifted to run Nov. 15 through Nov. 17, the better to accommodate the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, which is running yesterday and today in Shenzhen, China.

    ASEAN can also take pleasure in the fact that Trump has now attended two years running. Under previous administrations, the nonattendance of the U.S. president or senior U.S. officials was a running complaint.

    After all the hoopla, then, what did the visit add up to? Not much, it seems.

    Industry observers note that last year, when Kuala Lumpur hosted, the world was still gripped by questions about tariff negotiations. And Trump also got to play the peacemaker between Thailand and Cambodia—even though fighting between the two resumed the next month.

    It has been revealed that this time, no single problem defined the U.S. president’s visit, which lasted less than 24 hours. Trump proclaimed that the United States and Philippines had signed their biggest “ever” trade deal. But in typical Trump style, few details were forthcoming and nothing has actually been signed.

    On a symbolic level for Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., Trump’s arrival is a nice sign of the continued close relationship between the two countries.

    Recent findings suggest that manila’s previous president, Rodrigo Duterte, was deeply skeptical of the United States, flirting with ending the two countries’ alliance in favor of a deal with China. Marcos has spun the other way, doubling down on the security relationship with Washington to push back against Beijing.

    A few other deliverables were also duly delivered upon.

    Sources indicate that A set of deals involving anti-scam initiatives was finalized. A “trade deal” with Thailand—which, like the Philippines deal, was not actually a final agreement—was announced.

    Recent findings suggest that the leaders of the other Quad countries—Australia, Japan, and India—got a grand total of 55 scheduled minutes with Trump. The announcements that came out of that mainly repackaged old agreements.

    And Marcos arranged for some food from Jollibee—the Philippines’ top fast-food chain and a national icon—to be delivered to Trump in the interest of “providing extra energy for all the work that you have to do.”.

    At the state dinner, where Jollibee was not served, the U.S. president delivered a typically Trumpian speech. He assured ASEAN that he would support “partners and allies 100 percent,” adding that “when there’s a problem, you’ll call me.”.

    He also took the opportunity to praise Marcos for his “very good genetics” as well as calling on Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto to stand up for compliments.

    Sources indicate that some had expected announcements on Pax Silica, the United States’ global AI initiative. The United States is planning to build enormous semiconductor and data center facilities on land that used to house one of its military bases in the Philippines. But no announcements were forthcoming.

    According to recent reports, the Philippine government is keen on the idea as a way to boost its chips and electronics industry, as well as develop its defense industrial base. But the project is also controversial, spurring worries about the environmental impact and displacement of local people.

    Sources indicate that protesters took to the streets over Trump’s arrival to make their displeasure heard. Police reacted by blocking marches and detaining people. Nearly 300 demonstrators were arrested, according to protest organizers.

    Don’t read too much into this, though. The Philippines is one of the few countries in the world where Trump is still popular. A poll by Pew Research Centre found that 68 percent of Filipinos trusted Trump to do the right thing, the highest of any country surveyed.

    Overshadowing all of this was Trump’s next set of meetings in Shenzhen. Will he meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in a trilateral with Chinese President Xi Jinping? Maybe. Will he meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un? Also maybe.

    Sources indicate that so—at the end of the day—did Trump just stop by Manila for a pit stop, a photo op, and some Filipino fried food? Maybe.

    Not yet… Myanmar isn’t back in ASEAN, yet. Despite determined lobbying from Thailand, junta leader Min Aung Hlaing still wasn’t invited to attend the ASEAN summit.

    Since its 2021 coup, ASEAN has expressed its displeasure with Myanmar by not allowing junta leaders to attend summits. Senior civil servants get sent instead.

    However, a leaders’ statement adopted on Sunday declared that ASEAN would pursue “calibrated engagement with Myanmar” and “may consider the gradual restoration of Myanmar’s full political representation.”.

    The widespread assumption is that come 2028, when Thailand is the chair of the bloc, the final barriers will be removed.

    It has been revealed that the argument for reengagement is that, like it or not, the junta is there. Therefore, ASEAN countries need to engage—especially Thailand, which shares more than 2,000 kilometers of border with Myanmar.

    Recent findings suggest that critics will counter that engagement doesn’t seem to yield much. After the ASEAN summit, Min Aung Hlaing went on a rant in which he said that the statement on Myanmar was unreasonable. He also accused three unnamed member states of prejudice.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, in late October, fighting between junta forces and rebel groups on the Myanmar-Thia border saw explosives and shrapnel spill over to the Thai side. One Thai woman was wounded, and buildings were damaged.

    It has been revealed that not quite… The draft “Code of Conduct on the South China Sea,” which the Philippines pushed so hard for, wasn’t finished. According to Marcos in his press conference at the end of the summit, it’s 85 percent done, and all that’s left is the defining of terms.

    Industry observers note that with the actual terms as yet unknown, there is, on the summit sidelines, a good deal of cynicism. Even if the agreement is finished next year, many see two decidedly nonthrilling options.

    Sources indicate that one is that in order for China to sign the agreement, it will have to be extremely thin, with little newly introduced or binding terms in it. Second, if some reasonable guidelines are set out, China will just ignore them when it suits it.

    According to recent reports, an analyst from a country with its own massive claim on the waters suggested to me that a code of conduct could even be a disadvantage. If China breaks the rules, then other more rule-abiding countries might find their options to respond constrained by the agreement.

    Industry observers note that not on the agenda… Remember the Thailand-Cambodia conflict? ASEAN doesn’t, it seems.

    Following last summer’s fighting, ASEAN made an effort to address it. A Trump-sponsored peace deal was signed at the summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Following renewed fighting in December, an ASEAN observer team was revealed. And in Cebu, Philippines, earlier this year, the two countries met on the sidelines for Philippine-brokered talks, even if the results were limited.

    Recent findings suggest that this time around? Not a squeak. Partly to blame is perhaps that Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet didn’t attend. He was in Phnom Penh hosting the Francophonie Summit—see below.

    Sorry for the secondhand smoke. During the ASEAN summit, Prabowo apologized to Malaysia and Singapore for how they have been affected by the haze from Indonesia’s vast forest fires last month.

    He then rather undercut it by adding, “It is not our fault, but once again we apologize.”.

    Sources indicate that singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong also proposed that ASEAN should establish a joint task force to probe companies linked to such fires. This would expand on the current bilateral Singapore-Indonesia task force established last month following some diplomatic spats on the topic.

    Trade deals. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney dropped by on Saturday for the announcement that two trade deals were nearly done. Both an ASEAN-Canada and a Canada-Philippines trade deal have been forged with the aim of getting both signed next year.

    Recent findings suggest that how much free trade will actually be in these agreements? It’s hard to tell with no text published, but past experience suggests that any changes will probably be more incremental than sweeping.

    Wow, everything’s computer. On Saturday, ASEAN signed its Digital Economy Framework Agreement, which should come into force in early 2027. The proclaimed aim is to create an “interconnected ASEAN digital marketplace.”.

    Industry observers note that what does this mean in practice? The text’s not out yet, but this Singaporean government announcement lays out some broad strokes—mainly, accepting electronic trade documents, clearer rules on cross-border data flows, and a guarantee of no taxes on them for now, as well as cooperation on artificial intelligence and financial technology.

    Oil stockpile. Indonesia, Japan, the Philippines, and Thailand agreed to set up shared stockpiles of diesel and gasoline to help manage future energy crises. The actual facilities will be built in Indonesia and Thailand.

    It has been revealed that laos’s contestant, Thinla (center), performs during the grand final of the Eurovision Song Contest Asia 2026 at One Bangkok Forum in Bangkok on Nov. 14.Chanakarn Laosarakham/AFP via Getty Images.

    Cambodia: Cambodia hosted the Francophonie Summit from Saturday to Monday, gathering countries from across the French-speaking world—loosely defined. Prime Minister Hun Manet skipped ASEAN for this event and used it to do some diplomatic lobbying for Cambodia over its border dispute with Thailand, which infuriated the Thai government. French President Emmanuel Macron called for the investigation of the killing of a former opposition lawmaker and French Cambodian dual citizen Lim Kimya in Bangkok in 2025.

    Indonesia: Police raided a data center owned by Megaspeed and found empty server racks. Prabowo is expected to pick a loyalist from his own party to be the next VP. Online phenomenon iShowSpeed indicated off his Indonesian-speaking skills at an awards ceremony and then on a phone call with former U.S. President Barack Obama. And Nikkei has published a great article on Indonesia’s runners-for-hire who will burnish your Strava for you.

    Industry observers note that malaysia: The governing coalition faced another setback with a loss in the Melaka state election. And Macron visited on Tuesday and pitched cooperation on rare earths, weapons, semiconductors, and nuclear energy to reduce dependence on the United States and China.

    In a recent development, joseph Rachman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Southeast Asia Brief. He is a freelance journalist based in Bangkok. X: @rachman_joseph.

    In the wake of Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation as CEO of Nvidia over his alleged affair with a Chinese spy, the U.S. Commerce Department this week revealed latest export controls on artificial intelligence and semiconductors.     Sources indicate that in the wake of Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation as CEO of Nvidia over his alleged affair with a Chinese spy, the U.S. Commerce Department this week unveiled latest export controls on artificial intelligence and semiconductors. These rules mark the most serious effort to close the loopholes that have allowed Chinese companies to obtain access to U.S. chips and computing power. The new interim rules target three vulnerabilities: Chinese rerouting of U.S.-made AI chips through third countries, rented access to AI computing power, and Chinese chip designers’ ability to manufacture advanced chips at non-Chinese facilities.

    Industry observers note that the Nvidia scandal—including the alleged rerouting of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China and the Trump administration’s apparent quiescence—underscores the scope of the Chinese threat to U.S. artificial intelligence technology. The latest rules close crucial gaps, but they do not resolve the threat. The next area where the United States is especially exposed is the Gulf, where the most advanced U.S. chips are now arriving, to be utilized in data centers operated by partners that maintain extensive ties with China.

    The Gulf magnifies the Nvidia problem. Both the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia are trying to shift their economies away from oil, and they’re placing AI at the center of their strategies. In May 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump revealed that both countries would be able to purchase advanced U.S. chips to help facilitate these efforts. Abu Dhabi and Riyadh are financing massive AI buildouts, where Nvidia chips will be installed, operated, and even rented to customers or cloud tenants. The two monarchies are taking advantage of their desert land areas, access to lower-cost energy, and deep coffers, offering Nvidia an appealing market and affording Washington an opportunity to keep U.S. technology at the center of the AI buildout.

    According to recent reports, both the Saudis and the Emiratis, however, also maintain deep relations with China. Washington fears that Beijing could gain access, intentional or not, through its contractors or cloud customers—or via hardware or software that may be connected to U.S. systems or chips. Chinese infiltration could occur through a trusted partner, with or without their knowledge, without directly acquiring the restricted chips.

    Industry observers note that that’s why companies such as the UAE’s Group 42 have caught the eye of China watchers and technology hawks. The group’s past links to China and its tech sector, even though the manufacturer publicly renounced them after the Biden administration declared it a security risk, raise questions that diplomatic assurances cannot resolve. The problem is not what the company says but whether its operations, ownership, partnerships, and access to sensitive technology can be independently verified and insulated from possible Chinese exploitation.

    Industry observers note that saudi Arabia presents a similar challenge. The kingdom is pursuing AI autonomy by seeking control over every layer of the technology stack. But Washington will want evidence that Saudi officials can protect their data centers and cloud services from unauthorized access. And that case is increasingly difficult to make as Saudi Arabia continues to partner with both U.S. and Chinese technology companies.

    Industry observers note that the fresh rules make the Gulf an crucial litmus test for whether Washington can enforce its new approach in third-country data centers. Gulf-based facilities will need to prevent restricted consumers from accessing compute power enabled by U.S. chips, including indirectly through the cloud or other intermediaries. It’s not just about whether a Chinese organization or user can rent compute power through a Gulf partner, but also whether the safeguards are in place for partners who maintain U.S. compute power to verify ownership and the affiliations of users.

    U.S. export controls were designed for trade in tangible goods, but the Commerce Department has now acknowledged that simply controlling the physical movement of chips is not enough. The fresh rules extend export controls to some forms of remote access and computing power—intended, for example, to prevent a Chinese firm from renting access to a processor through a data center or cloud provider. The new rule is a major step forward but not a complete solution. Safeguarding U.S. chips will require more than protecting the physical product or regulating direct access. It will require oversight of the people and systems that can use the computing power that those chips provide. That means guarding not just the chips’ physical location but also their ownership, network architecture, and consumer access.

    Instead of determining which country or firm is purchasing a chip, an export policy will need to ask who will own and operate the facility, who can administer the compute power, which customers can rent its processors, what the networking and software infrastructure is made of, the nationality of consumers, and even whether the systems can be accessed outside of where they are housed. A processor being utilized in a Gulf data center, for example, may be used to provide computing power to a restricted Chinese tech giant or state institution through the cloud—so controls must follow the user, not just the export.

    In a recent development, nvidia sells the most advanced chips in the business. Its former CEO, who made himself the face of the organization’s strategy and government relations, was close with Trump and has decried more stringent export controls on AI chips, arguing that such restrictions will merely move more consumers toward Chinese suppliers like Huawei. His influence may have helped persuade Trump to sell limited amounts of the H200 chip to China. But the concern extends beyond Huang’s influence. Questions about the administration’s handling of the policy—including conflicts of interest involving U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Trump’s own financial interests in Nvidia, and other relationships between U.S. officials and companies that may have benefited from certain sales, like Jared Kushner’s—warrant a review of these decisions. Regulators should begin by reexamining the decision to allow the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to Saudi Arabia and the UAE.

    A new oversight policy would not entail a crackdown on Nvidia or a blanket ban on selling further advanced chips to Gulf states. Instead, Washington would expand access only when Gulf states meet specific conditions and establish guidelines for continuously evaluating who can access the technology. The new framework should become the baseline for future Gulf licenses that can identify approved facilities and consumers; limit chip quantities and aggregate compute power; prohibit restricted access and rentals; and require oversight of inventories, access logs, and control standards. Washington should also retain the right to suspend a license at any time. China has already sought to lease capacity through data centers in Europe and accessed U.S. chips to train its models through systems in Thailand.

    According to recent reports, when the Democrats take control of the U.S. Congress in January, they will likely press for tougher oversight of foreign chip deals—as they should. Democrats and Republicans have a considerable opportunity to work together on this matter. Even though this week’s new rules help address some of the areas of concern, they are an executive branch policy and thus subject to change at any moment. Congress can focus on passing the Remote Access Security Act, which will require export policy to include remote access controls, and the AI Overwatch Act, which will give Congress more oversight over foreign chip sales.

    For the UAE and Saudi Arabia, access to the most advanced chips is still possible but now comes with stronger U.S. demands—and any failure to adhere to those conditions should mean that access is immediately cut off. Fair or not, the Nvidia scandal raises the cost of assuming that trust is enough protection.

    It has been revealed that however, tighter U.S. restrictions also carry some risk. If U.S. requirements become too stringent, intrusive, costly, or unpredictable, Gulf governments may turn back toward Chinese tech or tilt toward other suppliers with fewer restrictions. Greater reliance on Chinese tech would not replace the U.S. technological edge overnight but over the long term, it could well reduce U.S. influence.

    The UAE and Saudi Arabia are seeking slightly different things. The UAE is leading the space in dealmaking and pushing the next generation of AI models, while Saudi Arabia is seeking to build out local compute capacity. For both, ongoing relationships with Chinese tech companies will remain an issue, and Washington will need stringent controls and verifications on who can access and use the systems.

    Industry observers note that china’s challenge to U.S. AI is a serious threat, and the United States must strengthen its technological defenses in the Gulf and elsewhere. The Commerce Department’s fresh rules are a meaningful step in closing the regulatory gap in U.S. export policy on chips. The Saudis’ and Emiratis’ AI ambitions make them key tests of whether the United States can enforce this approach. That requires systematic and continuous scrutiny of many more layers of the AI value chain than current U.S. export controls offer, including ownership, users, infrastructure, and remote access. The Saudis and Emiratis will, of course, say that they can be trusted. But in the post-Huang AI space, it is simply too risky to rely on assurances alone.

    Solar lease holdouts still see value in privately-owned residential projects

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (971 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Solarpowerworldonline

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The One Big Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects.
    • A residential solar project in Fresh York installed by Nickels Energy Solutions.
    • It has been revealed that after 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The One Big Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects. The ITC is a historic renewable energy subsidy that provides a 30% tax credit against the total cost of an eligible project, and it is currently available to the commercial and utility-scale solar segments.

    A residential solar project in Fresh York installed by Nickels Energy Solutions. Credit: Nickels Energy Solutions.

    It has been revealed that after 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned. However, a loophole in the tax credit language has allowed leased or “third party-owned” (TPO) solar projects to still receive the ITC (25D) on residential solar projects. In this scenario, it matters who owns the solar project, not necessarily where it’s built. The project can be subsidized because it is owned by a commercial tech giant, and not the homeowner.

    Some residential solar installers are still strictly pursuing and installing privately-owned solar projects. Nickels Energy Solutions (NES), a residential solar contractor working in Central New York believes a privately-owned PV system is still the better deal for the customer.

    “We don’t have the same offers as some of the bigger companies,” remarked Kevin Nickels, VP of sales with NES. “If you can offer leases, it’s like the ‘haves and have-nots.’ I don’t have that loophole or that trick up my sleeve, so it forces me to get the project sold, while I’m as sharp as I can be with margins to make it somewhat competitive.”.

    According to recent reports, TPO solar transactions are typically arranged at a lower up-front cost than a wholly owned solar project. Lease contract lengths vary by provider, and financiers have surety in these transactions because the projects will be built with products from an approved vendor list (AVL). Products on an AVL can qualify for a domestic content subsidy, another tax credit in addition to the ITC, because they are manufactured using a certain percentage of domestic components.

    In a recent development, these are premium products vetted for AVLs. But it can also mean that installers are paying premium prices for components in building TPO solar projects.

    Nickels believes that, while a privately owned residential solar project will cost more at the start, the combination of expensive components and interest rates for financing over a lease term — with factors like rate increases — can cost a customer more in the long run.

    “I don’t think all leases are bad,” he mentioned. “I just don’t think it’s what’s best for the industry or the homeowner.”.

    Selling residential solar in 2026.

    Rudy Wright, owner of Wright-Way Solar of Tyler, Texas, has shifted the organization’s focus from building upcoming projects to servicing existing systems. As the ITC exited the residential solar market, so did many of the lenders financing these projects. Without lending options, Wright-Way’s installation output has slowed down, and those clients who can afford solar are paying with cash or using a home equity loan to cover the cost.

    Despite that, Wright said he isn’t very interested in building leased solar projects.

    Wright-Way Solar built a solar plus storage project at a Ranch in Texas featuring arrays that are facing east, west and south. Credit: Wright-Way Solar.

    “I do think it cost me some of those entry level clients, but every time I analyzed the financing end of it, I felt like I was benefitting my company and the industry more than the customer,” Wright said. “I haven’t seen the angle where bringing a pre-purchase agreement or bringing a lease agreement has enough ironclad return for the customer.”.

    It has been revealed that tyler is a unique market for solar because many of Wright-Way’s customers are trying to make their properties more resilient, and less reliant on the grid, by installing solar and storage, and not just seeking cost savings for their energy use. Wright has installed solar plus storage systems on Texan ranches at a scale close a small commercial project.

    That promise of resilience is still enough reason for some people to commission a solar project in Texas, where the state’s independent electrical grid operator has faltered and experienced dangerous outages in recent years.

    “Folks realize money in the bank doesn’t do you any good if the power goes out,” Wright said.

    In a recent development, NES is still building a steady pipeline of residential solar projects in Upcoming York. Nickels said that has been possible in part because many of its clients are upper-middle class; but New York also maintains an incentive program for solar projects, NY-Sun, which includes a 25% state tax credit for residential systems.

    “The OBBBA caught a lot of states flat-footed,” Nickels mentioned. “Without federal support, it puts a lot of pressure on what the state is offering.”.

    Recent findings suggest that some states’ solar subsidy programs have stepped in where federal support has diminished since the OBBBA was passed. The North Carolina Clean Energy Technology Center maintains the Database of State Incentives for Renewables & Efficiency, which analyzes which states presently have policies and incentives supporting clean energy developments. Every state has policy enabling solar projects, but not necessarily cost incentives for individual projects.

    It has been revealed that while traditional residential solar projects have lost a significant subsidy, the reality is that energy costs have risen in response to new grid demands from hyperscale data centers and oil scarcity from the United States’ war in Iran. Sure, a privately owned residential solar project won’t receive the ITC, but it can still stabilize energy costs without them.

    “We lost a big incentive, but the rate increase is proportional,” Nickels said.

    Tech Report: Trump Is Facing a Very Different North Korea

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • BIEGUN was Deputy Secretary of State from December 2019 to January 2021 and Special Representative for North Korea from 2018 to 2021.
    • EMMA CHANLETT-AVERY is Senior Director for Political-Security Affairs and Deputy Director of the Washington office of the Asia Society Policy Institute.
    • According to recent reports, stephen E.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    STEPHEN E. BIEGUN was Deputy Secretary of State from December 2019 to January 2021 and Special Representative for North Korea from 2018 to 2021. He is a Distinguished Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

    EMMA CHANLETT-AVERY is Senior Director for Political-Security Affairs and Deputy Director of the Washington office of the Asia Society Policy Institute.

    And Now He Needs a Upcoming Strategy.

    According to recent reports, stephen E. Biegun and Emma Chanlett-Avery.

    In a recent development, donald Trump has Pyongyang on his mind. In recent months, the U.S. president has made comments to the media suggesting he is in communication with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. In an August 17 Truth Social post, for instance, Trump declared that the United States would scale back joint military drills with South Korea. The decision, he wrote, was “based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un,” describing the dictator as “unthreatening and respectful.”.

    Trump has not been subtle about his desire to restart diplomacy with Kim. With an eye on his legacy and the war with Iran stalemated, he is eager to notch a foreign policy win. During his first term, Trump held two historic U.S.–North Korean summits aimed at denuclearizing the Korean Peninsula—but both foundered because of the countries’ disparate expectations for the terms of a deal. Since his reelection, Trump has been looking to reopen talks with Kim. The ball is now in Pyongyang’s court, and Kim has signaled, if not an eagerness for renewed engagement, at least an unwillingness to rule it out. In August, after Trump insisted for the second time that he was in touch with Pyongyang, Kim Yo Jong—the leader’s influential sister—released a statement that read: “Regarding the reports from Washington about recent communication between the top leaders of North Korea and the U.S., I am completely unaware of such matters. It has been stated on numerous occasions that our head of state holds fond personal memories and positive feelings toward Trump. The relationship between the leaders remains excellent.” Although this is far from an agreement to meet, Kim Jong Un is not closing the door.

    In a recent development, if leader-to-leader talks materialize, Trump may believe his personal rapport with Kim will yield a deal. But he will be facing a very different North Korea than the one at their last meeting in 2019. The fallout from unfinished diplomacy during Trump’s first term, the COVID-19 pandemic, and global trends such as the sharp escalation in U.S.-Chinese strategic rivalry and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have destabilized the security landscape and created formidable obstacles to peaceful engagement. Meanwhile, North Korea’s continued nuclear and conventional military expansion and the growing support it is receiving from Moscow have strengthened Kim’s hand. Facing an emboldened Pyongyang, Trump can no longer fall back on the same concessions and negotiation tactics he used in previous talks.

    For a U.S.–North Korean summit to be successful, the United States must approach it with well-defined strategic goals and a clear understanding of what concessions it is willing to make. Washington should shift its focus away from denuclearization, at least in the short term, to concentrate on more achievable nuclear arms control and safety measures. The United States should also maintain a capable troop presence on the Korean Peninsula and reiterate its security assurances—particularly its nuclear-deterrence guarantees—to regional allies such as South Korea and Japan.

    Although diplomacy with North Korea has historically been difficult, Trump is eager to meet with Kim, and both sides want to avoid pushing the Indo-Pacific toward nuclear proliferation or all-out war. Careful engagement with Pyongyang could defuse tensions on the Korean Peninsula and lay the groundwork for a more stable security landscape.

    Sources indicate that since the U.S.–North Korean summit in 2019, the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have reshaped the Indo-Pacific in ways that strengthen Kim’s hand. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has drawn Washington’s focus away from Asia as, for the third time in the past quarter century, U.S. strategic attention and military assets have surged to the Middle East. The last American aircraft carrier stationed in the Indo-Pacific departed for the Persian Gulf in August, and U.S. strikes on Iran have rapidly depleted American munitions stockpiles. Washington’s Indo-Pacific allies, already strained by Trump’s abrupt policy shifts and punishing tariffs, are now concerned about deteriorating deterrence. Asian economies—many of which are deeply dependent on Middle Eastern energy supplies—have contracted as the Strait of Hormuz has remained compromised. Amid signs of further American retrenchment, U.S. allies and partners are increasingly skeptical about Washington’s commitment to the region.

    In a recent development, even more consequential is Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which has benefited North Korea in numerous ways. Moscow and Pyongyang’s once dormant relationship has flourished as Kim has sent thousands of munitions to replenish Russia’s depleted stockpiles and thousands of soldiers to fight and die in the ongoing ground war. Images of the new memorial to the Korean People’s Army soldiers who have perished in the invasion suggest an already significant loss of North Korean lives. In return, Pyongyang has received generous assistance from Moscow in violation of international sanctions, including abundant financial support for Kim’s regime and technology transfers that have enhanced North Korean military capabilities and may help Pyongyang more accurately deliver intercontinental ballistic missiles aimed at the United States. Russian patronage allows Kim to shower his regime’s elites with the economic benefits needed to cement their loyalty.

    According to recent reports, still, it is worth questioning how durable this partnership is. After more than four years of grinding warfare with no end in sight, Moscow is increasingly isolated and may be in a poor position to continue supporting Pyongyang. Russia’s preoccupation with Ukraine has allowed China to expand its presence in Central Asia, for instance, and Turkey to deepen its influence in Azerbaijan. Russian aggression has spurred Armenia and Moldova to look westward, and hundreds of thousands of young Russian men have fled the country to avoid military conscription while over a thousand Western companies have left. International sanctions are starving Russia of badly needed capital and technology, and Russian war policies have created huge imbalances and inflation, possibly with worse to come for the Russian economy. If North Korea continues to actively support Moscow in this war, and Russia fails or is defeated, the world will become a much more hostile place for Pyongyang.

    Recent findings suggest that russia and North Korea’s deepening ties have already begun to reshape China’s interests in the region. Beijing is still Pyongyang’s most vital partner, but the dynamic has changed considerably in recent years. Beijing previously saw denuclearization as a top priority on the Korean Peninsula—a shared objective, and at times a rare area of cooperation, with the United States. It disliked the destabilizing impact that North Korea’s pursuit of nuclear weapons had on tensions between the North and South and expended political capital responding to international condemnation of Pyongyang. Between 2006 and 2017, Beijing agreed to a series of UN Security Council resolutions that imposed sanctions and other restrictions on Pyongyang in response to six North Korean nuclear tests. Now, pressed to maintain its influence in Pyongyang amid a growing Russian–North Korean security relationship—and with the rest of the world distracted by other geopolitical crises—China has gone silent on the problem. When Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited North Korea in June to reassert his influence, denuclearization was not publicly mentioned. China’s upcoming approach will make U.S. engagement on this issue more challenging and risks driving other regional powers, such as South Korea and Japan, to reconsider their own policies on the deployment or development of nuclear weapons.

    According to recent reports, whether Pyongyang reengages with the United States may also depend on how much North Korea relies on China for economic support. Much of North Korean commerce passes through China, and although Beijing and Pyongyang’s relationship appears fairly stable, it remains wary and transactional, with each side skeptical of the other’s motives. North Korea may seek to reengage with the United States to counterbalance its overdependence on China, or as a hedge against Russia’s failure in its war with Ukraine. Conversely, as Trump and Xi upgrade and stabilize U.S.-Chinese relations, China could step in to broker the next Trump-Kim meeting.

    Industry observers note that the Kim dynasty has long vexed U.S. policymakers. Washington has sought multiple deals with North Korea, including during Trump’s first-term summits with Kim, but missteps and mistrust on both sides derailed them. Pyongyang has proved resilient to both U.S. and international sanctions. Indeed, during the COVID-19 pandemic, North Korea sealed its borders and deprived itself far more severely than sanctions could, yet it still survived. U.S. congressional interventions on human rights and humanitarian aid, meanwhile, have mostly failed to change North Korea’s behavior. Pyongyang has also cushioned the impact of sanctions by engaging in cybertheft, such as its $6.3 billion heist against the cryptocurrency exchange Binance this October. All the while, Pyongyang has steadily advanced its military capabilities and expanded its nuclear arsenal.

    In a recent development, although Washington’s previous attempts to rein in North Korea have failed, Trump’s renewed eagerness to meet with Kim and his unorthodox approach to foreign policy could provide a new opening for diplomacy. Trump has cultivated a direct relationship with Kim, shunning the bureaucratic negotiations that usually precede a deal. While a performative summit alone would be of little benefit to U.S. interests, Washington could use reengagement with Pyongyang to thaw inter-Korean relations and stabilize the peninsula by slowing or freezing North Korea’s nuclear buildup. Those goals may seem conventional, but as regional tensions worsen and Pyongyang’s nuclear arsenal grows, they are essential to averting potentially catastrophic conflict.

    Three questions cast a shadow over the possibility of renewed engagement between the United States and North Korea. First is the specific purpose of restarting engagement: What is the goal? Second is how to reopen communications. Despite Trump’s claims, there is no real proof that he has recently interacted with Kim. All evidence suggests the last contact between American and North Korean officials was in 2019, and it may be challenging to break a seven-year drought. Third is what are the incentives and tradeoffs the United States would be willing to consider as part of a negotiation—the same issue that bedeviled U.S. and North Korean officials in Hanoi.

    In a recent development, one possible formula for progress is focusing, at least temporarily, on steady arms control and international safety controls rather than the elusive goal of denuclearization. Denuclearization should remain Washington’s ultimate aspiration. But in the meantime, a North Korea awash with even more nuclear weapons makes the world only more dangerous. This approach will require serious diplomacy to minimize second-order consequences, particularly to avoid weakening U.S. alliances in the Indo-Pacific or triggering a collapse of the nuclear nonproliferation regime among nations that might see their only recourse as acquiring their own nuclear weapons. China, and perhaps even Russia, may concur with Washington on this point, and a shared desire to avoid more nuclear states in East Asia could help restart engagement.

    Industry observers note that kim has substantially more leverage now than in earlier encounters with Trump. Reopening communication will require using a mix of positive and negative assurances to convince him that he is unlikely to get a better chance to strike a deal. Kim may press the United States to scale back aspects of its cooperation with South Korea—such as joint military exercises and support for Seoul’s pursuit of nuclear-powered submarines—as preconditions for a meeting with Trump. Kim may even propose his own assurances of peace on the peninsula in exchange for a reduction of U.S. military forces in South Korea, although it is unclear whether Trump would agree to such conditions.

    In the worst-case scenario, Kim may take advantage of Trump’s eagerness to make a deal to extract weighty concessions from the United States. Kim has little reason to meet with Trump now, unless he calculates that he can secure major terms such as de facto recognition as a nuclear state, reduced sanctions, or a complete withdrawal of U.S. troops from the peninsula. Kim would likely insist that there be no discussion of denuclearization, North Korea’s support for the invasion of Ukraine, Pyongyang’s human rights abuses, or a final accounting for Japanese citizens kidnapped by North Korea under the rule of Kim Il Sung. Granting such concessions would end the U.S.–South Korean alliance.

    To ensure North Korea does not exploit the Trump administration, Washington must carefully consider what tradeoffs it is willing to make. Lifting sanctions, abandoning or delaying the denuclearization process, temporarily accepting North Korea as a nuclear state, and reducing the U.S. military presence in South Korea are all long-standing demands of Kim’s regime that are likely on the table. Although lifting international sanctions would require UN Security Council consensus, Trump may be willing to reduce unilateral U.S. sanctions, which he considers an obstacle to better bilateral relations and which have been ineffective in stemming Pyongyang’s nuclear advances.

    Although denuclearization has been a major talking point for U.S. administrations since the early 1990s, the Trump administration may need to set it aside, at least in the short term. Pyongyang’s nuclear capabilities have increased since Trump’s 2018 and 2019 summits with Kim, suggesting that the stalemate caused by continued U.S. demands for the full-scale dismantlement of North Korea’s nuclear program may have given Kim time and space to grow his arsenal. Even if denuclearization remains a long-term U.S. priority—and it should—pragmatism is essential to reducing the threat posed by Kim’s regime. In exchange for stepping away from denuclearization, Trump should demand that Kim freeze any further expansion of his arsenal and explore possibilities for greater strategic stability, including renewed inter-Korean dialogue, transparency and confidence-building efforts, security measures that bolster nuclear facilities’ safety and guard against accidents, and strict adherence to nonproliferation. Trump must make it clear to Kim that an unconstrained expansion of North Korea’s nuclear arsenal will pressure South Korea and Japan to deploy nuclear weapons on their territory and possibly develop their own.

    Regardless of Kim’s demands, the United States must preserve its troop presence on the Korean Peninsula and continue joint military exercises with South Korea as long as the threat of North Korean aggression persists. The mantra of U.S. troops in South Korea is “ready to fight tonight.” Joint military exercises keep U.S. and South Korean forces prepared for combat, which is essential to deterring North Korean attacks. It would be dangerous and irresponsible to send American soldiers, sailors, marines, and airmen to the peninsula without ensuring peak readiness. Instead of withdrawing troops, the United States should offer confidence-building measures to North Korea—practices that reduce the risk of conflict breaking out because of misjudgment. These could include military-to-military engagement and security reassurances among the United States, South Korea, and North Korea, or greater transparency around military exercises—allowing observers on a reciprocal basis, for example. Sustaining Washington’s alliance with South Korea and avoiding cascading nuclear proliferation are critical to U.S. interests in the region. American negotiators must remind Kim that the U.S. military presence and its extended nuclear-deterrence guarantees for Seoul and Tokyo hold back even larger conventional military—and possibly nuclear—buildups in the region.

    In a recent development, finally, North Korea and the United States—and perhaps, in time, South Korea and Japan—should sustain diplomatic engagement by agreeing to assign diplomats to each other’s capitals through reciprocal liaison offices, which would maintain relations without granting full diplomatic recognition. In 2018 and 2019, the two sides discussed housing such diplomats in the German Embassy in Pyongyang and the Swedish Embassy in Washington. Liaison offices would also stabilize and prolong the communication necessary to quietly work through complex negotiations.

    If North Korea rejects Trump’s overtures, the United States is not without options. Washington could pressure the Kim regime by intensifying the scale and tempo of joint military exercises with South Korea; deploying American armaments, including short-range ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and possibly nuclear weapons, to South Korea and Japan; and pursuing a new campaign to choke off North Korea’s economic resources through sanctions and interdiction. The United States could also deploy additional air defense assets to Japan and South Korea, including THAAD air defense radar systems and interceptors. Washington and its allies could dramatically expand efforts to undermine Kim’s rule by mounting sustained criticisms of North Korea’s dangerously large nuclear weapons arsenal and its use of international criminal enterprise to steal from and economically defraud other nations, which could spur other countries to curb their material or diplomatic support for North Korea or more aggressively sanction Kim’s regime.

    Beyond short-term negotiations, a fourth question is less complicated but just as important: What role should Japan and South Korea play in U.S. engagements with North Korea? Many past administrations, both Republican and Democratic, have considered coordination with allies essential to establishing a durable solution on the Korean Peninsula. But Trump’s antipathy toward alliances suggests close consultation with South Korea and Japan is unlikely. Their absence from the negotiating table may actually accelerate U.S.–North Korean engagement, because coordination across allied governments can be unwieldy and slow, and Pyongyang has not been receptive to past overtures by Seoul and Tokyo. Although South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi both rhetorically back engagement with North Korea, Pyongyang has bluntly rejected their outreach.

    Even if Seoul and Tokyo are not directly engaged in U.S.–North Korean diplomacy, they would still likely welcome a U.S.-led deal with Kim if it protects their core security interests. But a deal with Kim that ignores American allies’ concerns would be dangerous. South Korea harbors an appetite to develop its own nuclear arsenal, particularly if it feels U.S. security protections are receding. Should Seoul move in that direction, Tokyo would almost certainly reconsider its own nonnuclear status, potentially igniting a nuclear arms race in Asia. Given North Korea’s long-standing hostility toward both Japan and South Korea, proliferation would destabilize the Indo-Pacific and leave the global nonproliferation regime in tatters.

    Any deal, even one that addresses Seoul’s and Tokyo’s core interests, will likely need to be paired with American security reassurances to allies’ governments and publics. Japan and South Korea must continue building their own conventional defense capabilities while the United States sustains its commitment to defending its Asian allies—especially extended nuclear deterrence. The United States must pursue delicate, nuanced diplomacy to avoid creating a stronger, legitimized North Korea; straining its alliances with Seoul and Tokyo; and debilitating the international nonproliferation regime.

    Sources indicate that despite the risks of U.S.–North Korean engagement, the time may be ripe to break the diplomatic paralysis that has allowed Pyongyang to advance its military capabilities for so long. The last two years of Trump’s presidency—particularly his summitry calendar in late 2026—will bring him to Asia, potentially facilitating a meeting with Kim. Such a visit would present the best chance for the kind of performative, high-profile meeting that both Trump and Kim favor.

    Trump is the ultimate iconoclast in traditional great-power politics, as evidenced by his shifting relationships with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin, which could shape Washington’s engagement with Pyongyang. Still, there may be a way to leverage Trump’s affection for Kim, and Kim’s recent restraint in criticizing the United States, to outline a deal that arrests the growing threat of North Korean nuclear weapons.

    Sources indicate that the bruising Republican defeat in the U.S. midterm elections could also change North Korea’s diplomatic calculus, especially because it suggests Trump’s political standing in the United States has faltered, and he may struggle to deliver the results Kim seeks. Trump may force the glitch, however, and propose a meeting with Kim after the November Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit in Shenzhen, China. It would not be surprising for Trump to suggest that this meeting take place in Pyongyang, putting Kim on the spot. If leader-to-leader talks occur, both sides should remember the central lesson from Trump’s first-term summits: engagement without sufficient preparation and clearly defined goals is not enough to strengthen security and stability on the Korean Peninsula.

    Growing tensions in the Indo-Pacific raise the prospect of a much darker future, where conditions on the Korean Peninsula remain unchanged and Asia’s entanglements in European and Middle Eastern conflicts metastasize into a new world war—perhaps ignited in Taiwan, the South China Sea, or the Korean Peninsula. Even if no war breaks out, in just a few years the United States could find itself in a world where Asia’s five current nuclear states are joined by two, three, or more new players.

    But this future is not inevitable. All the leaders engaged in North Korean security debates—from Lee and Takaichi to Xi and Putin—want to avoid such escalation. Even the North Koreans surely recognize this is the most dangerous path. This shared goal means diplomacy is still possible, despite formidable challenges. For all Trump’s idiosyncrasies, one should take his desire to peacefully end tensions on the Korean Peninsula at face value. He has made his intentions clear. What happens next is up to Chairman Kim.
